The dominant tenement is benefited; the servient tenement is burdened. Students confuse these constantly, and the memory aid is that the servient parcel serves the other.

An easement appurtenant passes with the dominant parcel whether or not it is mentioned in the deed, which is why the "together with" language in Lesson 04 matters for clarity rather than for creation — and why a landlocked parcel's access must be traced in the records rather than assumed from the description.

3.3 How easements are created

MethodHow it arises
Express grantThe servient owner grants it in writing
Express reservationA grantor conveys land and reserves an easement over it
ImplicationArising from the circumstances of a division of land, where prior use was apparent and continuous
NecessityArising where a parcel would otherwise be landlocked by the division that created it
PrescriptionArising from long use that meets the legal requirements
DedicationA private owner devoting land to public use, accepted by the public body
CondemnationAcquired by a government body exercising eminent domain

The last several are legal doctrines with requirements a licensee cannot evaluate. Recognition is the skill; whether a prescriptive or implied easement exists is a question for counsel.

3.4 The licensee's practical problem

The recurring situation is not exotic:

The preliminary report shows a ten-foot utility easement along the rear property line. The buyer intends to build a workshop at the rear of the lot.

What the licensee does: obtain the underlying document, ensure the buyer reviews it — width, location, permitted use, maintenance obligations — and route the effect on his plans to counsel and to the jurisdiction, before the contingency expires.

What the licensee does not do: call the easement routine because most properties have one; ask the title company to "remove" it, which misunderstands what an exception is; or predict that the workshop "should be fine."

An easement along the rear line can prevent exactly the structure this buyer is buying the property to build. That is not a formality.

3.5 Licenses

A license is permission to use another's land that is generally revocable and does not create an interest in the land.

EasementLicense
Interest in landYesNo
RevocableGenerally notGenerally yes
Runs with the landYesNo
Requires writingGenerally yesNot necessarily

The neighbor who has been allowed to park in the driveway for years has, in the ordinary case, a license — not an easement. But long use can raise a prescriptive claim, which is why "we've always let them" is a sentence a licensee should route rather than resolve.

3.6 Termination

Easements can end by express release, by merger of the dominant and servient parcels in one owner, by expiration of a stated term, by abandonment where the requirements are met, or by the purpose becoming impossible.

Non-use alone generally does not terminate an easement. A client who says "nobody has used that road in twenty years, so it's gone" has stated a conclusion the law usually does not reach. Route it.

3.7 A worked easement problem

The property. A residential lot. The preliminary report lists: a public utility easement along the rear ten feet, recorded 1958; an easement for ingress and egress in favor of the adjoining parcel, recorded 1974, described as a twenty-foot strip along the northern boundary; and a drainage easement in favor of the county, recorded 1991.

The buyer intends to build a detached workshop in the rear yard and to fence the north side.

What each easement means for his plan.

The utility easement. Section 3.2's easement in gross — it benefits a utility rather than a neighboring parcel. A structure built within it is a structure built where someone else has a recorded right of access, and the practical consequence is not theoretical: excavation, repair, or replacement can require removal.

The ingress and egress easement. Appurtenant, benefiting the adjoining parcel, and it runs with the land — meaning it does not end because the current neighbor is friendly or because the strip is not currently used. The fence the buyer plans would obstruct a recorded right of access, which is the fact pattern of a neighbor dispute and possibly of an injunction.

The drainage easement. Benefiting a public entity, with its own scope defined by the instrument.

What the licensee does — and Section 3.4 defines the boundary precisely.

He obtains the recorded instruments, not the one-line summaries in the report. The summaries state that an easement exists; the instruments state what it permits, where exactly it runs, and what it prohibits. This is the single most valuable thing a licensee does with a preliminary report and the thing most often skipped.

He tells the buyer his stated plans are affected by items in the report, identifies which ones, and recommends in writing that he review them with counsel and, for location, obtain a survey.

He recommends the buyer confirm with the jurisdiction what may be built where, because Lesson 06's public controls operate independently of these private ones — and a plan can be defeated by either.

What the licensee does not do.

He does not interpret the instruments. Whether the 1974 easement permits a gate, whether the 1958 easement has been abandoned by non-use, and whether anything about the arrangement has changed by operation of law are legal questions, and Section 3.6's termination doctrines are exactly the kind of analysis a licensee must not perform for a client.

He does not reassure. "That easement is ancient, nobody uses it" is the sentence that appears in the complaint.

The professional summary. The buyer is buying a lot on which he cannot do two of the things he intends without answering questions first. He is entitled to know that before he removes his contingencies, and the licensee's contribution is that he learns it on day three rather than after closing.

3.9 How easements are created, and how they end

Section 3.2 defined the easement. Its creation and termination are where the practical questions sit, because an easement nobody granted in writing is the one that surprises a buyer.

Creation.

MethodHow it arisesWhat a licensee sees
Express grant or reservationThe owner grants it, or reserves it when conveyingA recorded instrument; a Schedule B exception
ImplicationA prior use, apparent and continuous, reasonably necessary, existing when a parcel was dividedNothing recorded — a driveway or a sewer line crossing a neighbour
NecessityA parcel is landlocked by a division of formerly common ownershipA parcel with no frontage on any road
PrescriptionOpen, notorious, hostile, continuous use for the statutory periodA neighbour who has used the driveway for twenty years
DedicationAn owner offers land for public use and it is acceptedStreets and public ways on a subdivision map

The last three create rights nobody recorded, which is why the standard title policy excepts "any facts an accurate survey would disclose" and why Assignment 09 Section 4.9 insists that possession is notice.

Termination.

Express release. The dominant owner releases it, in writing, recorded.

Merger. The dominant and servient tenements come into the same ownership. An easement over one's own land is not an easement — and note the consequence: if the parcels are later separated again, the easement does not automatically revive.

Abandonment. Non-use alone is generally not enough; there must be conduct showing intent to abandon.

Expiration. Where the instrument sets a term or a condition that has occurred.

End of necessity. An easement by necessity ends when the necessity does — when the landlocked parcel gains other access.

3.10 A worked easement problem

A buyer is purchasing a rural parcel. The preliminary report shows a recorded 20-foot access easement from the county road across a neighbouring parcel. On inspection, the actual driveway runs about 60 feet to the north of where the recorded easement is described, and has evidently done so for many years — there is mature landscaping along it and a culvert under it.

The buyer has two different access questions and only one of them is answered by the recorded easement.

The recorded easement is real and gives a legal right of access — over ground that has no road on it. Building a driveway within the recorded easement would mean grading a new route, and the neighbour's landscaping and outbuildings may be in the way.

The driveway in use is not within the recorded easement. Its legal basis, if any, would be prescription, implication, or an unrecorded agreement — none of which appears in the report and none of which a licensee can determine.

Three actions, in order. Obtain the recorded easement instrument and read its description. Have a surveyor locate both the recorded easement and the existing driveway on the ground. Then send the result to counsel, because whether the buyer may keep using the existing driveway is a legal question with a factual foundation that only the survey supplies.

What makes this urgent rather than interesting. If the buyer's use of the actual driveway rests on prescription against the neighbour, the purchase itself may affect it, and a neighbour who has tolerated one family's use for twenty years may take a different view of a new owner. The time to find out is during the contingency period.

The failure mode to avoid is the reassuring summary: "there's a recorded easement, you have access." That sentence is true, is what the report says, and completely misses what is actually happening on the ground.

3.11 Checkpoint

You should be able to identify the dominant and servient parcels, distinguish an easement from a license, and state the correct handling of an easement shown in a preliminary report.

4. Deed restrictions and covenants

4.1 What they are

Private restrictions limit what may be done with land, created by agreement and recorded so that they bind successive owners.

They appear as conditions or restrictions in individual deeds, and — far more commonly in modern practice — as a recorded declaration of covenants, conditions, and restrictions governing a subdivision or common interest development.

4.2 Private restrictions versus zoning

This distinction is worth stating precisely, because clients get it wrong in a costly direction.

Private restrictionsZoning
SourcePrivate agreement, recordedGovernment, by ordinance
Enforced byOwners, or the associationThe jurisdiction
Changed byThe procedure in the instrument, often requiring owner approvalThe land use process
Effect on each otherNeither overrides the other

The controlling proposition: where zoning and a recorded restriction differ, the more restrictive generally governs in practice.

Zoning permitting a duplex does not authorize one where the recorded restrictions prohibit it. A restriction permitting a second unit does not authorize one where zoning prohibits it. A buyer must satisfy both.

A licensee who tells a buyer the property is "zoned for it, so you're fine" has answered half the question.

4.3 What restrictions commonly cover

Use — residential only, no business, no short-term rental. Building — setbacks, height, materials, minimum size, architectural approval. Appearance — paint, landscaping, fencing, visible vehicles. Occupancy and animals. Rental limits, including caps on the number of rented units, which can affect both an investor buyer and financing availability.

4.4 Enforcement

Private restrictions are enforced by those entitled to enforce them — other owners in the scheme, or the association. Remedies commonly include injunctive relief and, in an association context, the association's own enforcement mechanisms.

Restrictions that violate law are not enforceable. Racially restrictive covenants, discussed in Lesson 14, still appear in the recorded language of older title chains and are unenforceable and void. Their presence in a chain of title is not a defect in the seller's title, and California provides a process for their restrictive language to be addressed.

A licensee encountering such language should recognize what it is, not repeat it, and route the question of what may be done about it.

4.5 What a licensee may and may not do

May: identify that restrictions exist; obtain the recorded documents; ensure the buyer receives and reviews them; point out that they bind him regardless of zoning; recommend counsel where their effect on his plans matters; and document the recommendation.

May not: summarize the declaration for the buyer as though the summary were the document; opine on whether a particular use is permitted; predict whether an association will approve something; or characterize a restriction as unenforceable.

A buyer asks: "Can I run my business out of the garage?"

Correct: "There are two separate questions — what the city allows and what the recorded restrictions allow, and you have to satisfy both. Here are the CC&Rs; the use article starts on page eleven. The city's planning counter answers the zoning half. I'd get both answers before your contingency expires, and I'll note that we discussed it."

Incorrect: "It's a quiet business, nobody will care."

4.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to explain why zoning permission is not sufficient, and answer a permitted-use question correctly.

5. Encroachments, priority, and recording

5.1 Encroachments

An encroachment is an improvement extending onto another's land — a fence, an eave, a driveway, a retaining wall, a structure.

Encroachments raise a mixture of questions no licensee can resolve: whose land it is on, whether the encroaching owner has acquired rights through long use, whether removal can be compelled, and what the effect is on marketability.

The licensee's obligations: disclose what is observed; recommend a survey where the facts call for one; recommend counsel where a claim may exist; document; and ensure it happens before the contingency expires.

What the licensee must not do: state where the boundary is, characterize the encroachment as minor, predict whether the neighbor has a claim, advise moving a fence to resolve it, or tell a buyer that decades of use have settled the question.

5.2 The recording system

California maintains a public record of documents affecting real property, and the system exists to answer one question: who has notice of what?

Type of noticeWhat it is
Actual noticeThe person in fact knows
Constructive noticeThe law charges the person with knowing, because it was recorded
Inquiry noticeFacts that would prompt a reasonable person to investigate — such as someone visibly in possession who is not the record owner

Recording gives constructive notice to the world. That is the whole mechanism: a recorded document is knowable by anyone who looks, so the law treats everyone as knowing it.

Inquiry notice deserves attention because it is the one that surprises people. A buyer who sees an occupant who is not the seller, or a well-worn path across the rear of the lot, has facts that would prompt investigation — and may be charged with what the investigation would have revealed, recorded or not.

5.3 Priority

The general rule: first in time, first in right — as measured by recording, for those entitled to the recording system's protection.

The exceptions are what matter in practice:

ExceptionEffect
Property tax liensGenerally take priority regardless of when they attached
Mechanics liensPriority is measured from commencement of the work rather than from the lien's own recording date — ahead of what attached after the work began, behind what was already attached (Civil Code § 8450)
Subordination agreementA lienholder agrees to take a lower position than it would otherwise hold
Purchase-money priorityCertain purchase-money security interests receive favored treatment

Subordination is the one licensees encounter most. A construction lender frequently requires the seller who carried financing to subordinate, moving the seller behind the construction loan. Whether to agree is a significant decision with real consequences, and it belongs to counsel — not to the licensee explaining that "it's standard."

5.4 Why priority determines outcomes

Priority determines who is paid first from a limited fund and whose interest survives a foreclosure. A junior lienholder wiped out by a senior foreclosure has lost its security, whatever the merits of the debt.

That is why the recording date on the preliminary report is not administrative detail. It is the order in which the property's value is claimed.

5.5 What escrow and title actually do with this

Escrow obtains payoff demands and clears what must be cleared; title determines what it will insure and what it will except. Neither advises the parties, and neither decides a dispute.

A licensee's contribution is to surface issues early — the recent construction, the similar-name judgment, the unreleased deed of trust — so there is time to resolve them, and to route the questions rather than answering them.

5.7 Priority worked as a payment waterfall

Section 5.3 stated the priority rule — first in time, first in right, subject to statutory exceptions. This section runs it as arithmetic, because that is how it is experienced.

The two exceptions that outrank recording order.

Property tax liens. Revenue and Taxation Code § 2192.1 puts it without qualification: every tax declared a lien on real property, and every public improvement assessment declared by law to be a lien, "have priority over all other liens on the property, regardless of the time of their creation" — over "any recognizance, deed, judgment, debt, obligation, or responsibility" the property may become charged with. A first deed of trust recorded in 2004 is junior to a 2026 property tax lien, and no recording date changes that.

Mechanics liens are measured from commencement of the work. Civil Code § 8450 states the rule and its limit in one sentence:

"(a) A lien under this chapter, other than a lien provided for in Section 8402, has priority over a lien, mortgage, deed of trust, or other encumbrance on the work of improvement or the real property on which the work of improvement is situated, that (1) attaches after commencement of the work of improvement or (2) was unrecorded at the commencement of the work of improvement and of which the claimant had no notice.

(b) Subdivision (a) is subject to the exception provided for in Section 8452."

Read what the section gives the lien priority over, because it is a closed list. An encumbrance that attached after commencement of the work; or one that was unrecorded when the work commenced and of which the claimant had no notice. That is all of it. An encumbrance already attached and of record when the first bulldozer arrived is on neither branch, and the mechanics lien does not reach it.

So relation-back is a measuring point, not a promotion to first position. The lien's priority is taken from the day work commenced instead of the day the claim of lien was recorded. It moves the lien back in time; it does not move it to the front of the line. A lien whose work commenced in 2023 competes as a 2023 interest — ahead of everything that attached in 2024 and after, and behind everything already attached in 2019 and 2022.

This is why a construction lender inspects the site before recording. A lender who records after work has begun has attached after commencement, is inside § 8450(a)(1), and may find itself junior to a lien not recorded for months. A lender who records before anyone breaks ground is outside the subdivision entirely. It is also why title companies ask about recent work: the question is not whether a lien is on record, it is whether one can still arrive with an earlier date than the buyer's lender.

Two limits the section names, and a licensee who quotes subdivision (a) alone has quoted half a rule. § 8450(a) excepts "a lien provided for in Section 8402" — the lien of a person who provides work for a site improvement — whose priority is set separately by § 8458. And § 8450(b) makes the whole rule subject to § 8452, under which a mortgage or deed of trust that would otherwise be subordinate takes priority over a lien for work provided after the recording of a payment bond that refers to it and is in an amount not less than 75 percent of its principal. Neither operates in the ordinary example below.

The waterfall. A property sells at a forced sale for $742,000, with five liens recorded against it.

RecordedLienAmount
2019First deed of trust$520,000
2022Second deed of trust (HELOC, full line)$150,000
2024Abstract of judgment$88,000
2025Mechanics lien (work commenced 2023)$61,000
2026Property taxes$9,300

Order of payment, and why:

OrderLienWhy it sits herePaidRunning balance
1Property taxes 2026Priority over all other liens regardless of the time of their creation — R&T § 2192.1$9,300$732,700
2First deed of trust 2019Attached four years before the work commenced — on neither branch of § 8450(a)$520,000$212,700
3Second deed of trust 2022Attached a year before the work commenced — on neither branch of § 8450(a)$150,000$62,700
4Mechanics lien — measured from 2023Ahead of what attached after commencement$61,000$1,700
5Abstract of judgment 2024Attached after the 2023 commencement — § 8450(a)(1)$1,700 of $88,000$0

Three results worth sitting with.

Relation-back did not move the mechanics lien to the front, and nothing in § 8450 would have let it. The lien was recorded last of the five and is paid fourth. The 2019 first deed of trust and the 2022 HELOC were both attached and of record in 2023 when the work commenced, so neither "attaches after commencement" nor was "unrecorded at the commencement," and the section reaches neither. A licensee who remembers relation-back as "the mechanics lien comes first" will get this backwards, and the mistake is expensive in exactly the case where it matters.

What relation-back actually did is visible in one line. The mechanics lien was recorded in 2025 and the abstract of judgment in 2024, so on recording order alone the judgment would be paid first. It is not. The lien is measured from 2023, the judgment attached after that, and § 8450(a)(1) puts the lien ahead of it. Change one fact — commencement in 2025 rather than 2023 — and the judgment creditor is paid in full and the contractor takes the $1,700.

The judgment creditor recovers $1,700 of $88,000 and the lien is extinguished by the sale. Junior liens are wiped by a senior foreclosure; the debt survives as a personal obligation where the anti-deficiency statutes do not bar it, but the security is gone.

5.8 What a licensee does with a preliminary report

The waterfall above is invisible until someone reads Schedule B, and reading it is a licensee's job in the sense that noticing is the licensee's job.

Four things to look for, in order.

Anything the seller did not mention. A second deed of trust, an abstract of judgment, a mechanics lien, a lis pendens, a bankruptcy. Sellers routinely forget encumbrances that were resolved informally and never released of record.

Anything with a date close to the present. A recent recording is a live situation. A mechanics lien recorded last month means a contractor is unpaid now, and there may be more coming from other trades on the same job.

Anything naming a person who is not the seller. A judgment against a former owner with the same surname; a lien against a business the seller once operated. Some of these are genuine and some are name-match errors, and the difference is resolved by a title officer, not by the licensee's judgment about which it looks like.

Anything about boundaries, access or easements. These do not get paid off at closing. They travel with the land, and they change what the buyer is buying.

And one habit that costs nothing. Send the preliminary report to the buyer with the items numbered and a sentence asking which they want explained. It converts a document that is routinely unread into a document with a record of delivery — and if the buyer later says nobody told them about the easement, the email is the answer.

5.9 Checkpoint

You should be able to explain constructive and inquiry notice, state the priority rule and its principal exceptions, and describe the correct handling of an encroachment.

6. Title exceptions and risk allocation

6.1 What a preliminary report is

A preliminary report reports the condition of title as shown in the records and states the terms on which the title insurer would be willing to issue a policy, including the exceptions it would take.

Three things it is not:

  • Not a guarantee that title is clear.
  • Not the policy. It states terms; the policy is the contract.
  • Not a survey. It addresses record title, not the physical property.

6.2 What an exception means

The single most useful sentence in this lesson:

An exception is an item the policy will not insure against. The buyer bears that risk unless it is otherwise addressed.

That is why exceptions are read rather than skimmed, and why the underlying recorded documents must be obtained. An exception naming a recorded easement tells the buyer that an easement exists; only the document tells him where it runs, how wide it is, and what it permits.

6.3 Exclusions and requirements

Two related concepts:

Exclusions are categories the policy form does not cover at all — commonly including governmental regulation such as zoning, the exercise of eminent domain, and matters created or agreed to by the insured.

Requirements are what the insurer needs before issuing — a reconveyance, a resolution, a release, evidence of authority.

A licensee reading a preliminary report should distinguish the three: exceptions are risks not insured, exclusions are categories outside the policy, and requirements are things that must be done before closing. The requirements are the ones with deadlines attached.

6.4 Reading the report item by item

ItemCorrect handling
Utility easement along the rear lineObtain the document; width, location, permitted use. Can prevent structures the buyer intends
Recorded CC&RsObtain and review; bind the buyer regardless of zoning
Unreleased deed of trust the seller says was paidA recorded reconveyance must be obtained; recollection does not clear the record
Mechanic's lienRoute to escrow and title; note that priority may relate back
Judgment against a similarly named personRoute to title for resolution; do not assume it is or is not the seller
Lis pendensRecognize as a serious cloud; route to counsel
Item the buyer does not understandRefer

Three responses that are wrong in every case: treating an item as routine because most properties have one; asking the title company to "remove" an exception; and predicting the practical effect of an easement or restriction on the buyer's plans.

6.5 Owner's and lender's policies

The owner's policy insures the buyer's interest. The lender's policy insures the lender's lien and its priority. They insure different interests, which is why both commonly exist, and why a buyer who declines an owner's policy because "there's a title policy on the loan" has misunderstood what he is not buying.

Extended coverage may address matters a standard policy excepts, including some survey matters, typically requiring a survey or other evidence. Whether to obtain it is the buyer's decision, informed.

6.6 The timing point

The preliminary report and the underlying documents belong at the front of the transaction queue, with the association documents and the hazard-area insurance quotes.

An exception discovered late — an easement across the building site, an unreleased lien requiring a document from a lender that no longer exists — takes time to resolve. A buyer who receives the report on day three has options; one who receives it on day twelve of a fourteen-day review has a formality.

6.7 A worked preliminary report

The report on a suburban residence, in the order the items appear:

  1. General and special taxes for the current fiscal year, a lien not yet due and payable.
  2. A supplemental assessment.
  3. A bond or assessment district obligation.
  4. Covenants, conditions and restrictions recorded 1964, with a note that any provision restricting on a protected basis is void and unenforceable.
  5. An easement for public utilities, 1964.
  6. A deed of trust, 2019, securing an original amount, in favor of a named lender.
  7. A second deed of trust, 2021, in favor of a different lender.
  8. A notice of a pending action affecting the property, recorded four months ago.
  9. A judgment against a person whose name is similar to the seller's.
  10. Requirements: satisfactory evidence of the authority of the parties, and a statement regarding parties in possession.

How a licensee reads this, applying Sections 6.2 through 6.4.

Items 1 through 3 are cost items, and the buyer's monthly figure has probably not included the third. Section 6.4's discipline is to read every item rather than the ones that look important.

Item 4 is a private restriction, and it is separate from zoning. Section 4.2. The unenforceable-provision note is standard and does not make the remaining provisions unenforceable — which is precisely the misreading a licensee must not encourage. Obtain the document; route its interpretation.

Item 5 is located from the instrument rather than assumed.

Items 6 and 7 are monetary liens expected to be paid at closing. Two deeds of trust means two payoff demands, and Lesson 10 of the practice course explains why the good-through date on each matters.

Item 8 is the most serious item on the report. A recorded notice of a pending action puts the world on notice of a claim affecting the property. It is not cleared by paying it, its resolution depends on the underlying matter, and it can affect insurability and financing. This is escalated to the broker and the title officer immediately — and it raises a disclosure question for the seller that the licensee does not answer alone.

Item 9 is the similar-name judgment. Section 5.3's priority rules make this consequential if it is the seller. The title company resolves it through its process, and the licensee's contribution is flagging it early rather than discovering on day twenty-five that clearance takes time.

Item 10's requirements are not exceptions. Section 6.3's distinction. They are conditions the title company will insist on before issuing, and the authority requirement is Lesson 03's ownership question arriving from the title side.

What the licensee does with the whole document. Deliver it promptly with delivery evidenced; obtain the underlying recorded instruments for items 4 and 5; flag items 8, 9, and 10 to escrow, the broker, and the client in writing; recommend review with counsel; and record what was recommended and when.

What he does not do. Rank the items by seriousness for the client as legal advice, tell the buyer item 8 "will probably clear," characterize the 1964 restrictions, or forward the report with "let me know if you have questions." Section 6.6's timing point is the reason: a report delivered without the recommendation that it be reviewed has been delivered in a way that does not produce a review.

6.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to explain what an exception means, distinguish exceptions from exclusions and requirements, and state the correct response to each item on a preliminary report.

Key terms

TermDefinition
EncumbranceA right or interest held by someone other than the owner, affecting title or use. Travels with the property.
Money encumbrance (lien)An encumbrance securing a debt against the property.
Non-money encumbranceAn encumbrance affecting use — easements, recorded restrictions, encroachments.
Voluntary lienCreated by the owner's agreement, typically a deed of trust.
Involuntary lienArising by operation of law without consent — taxes, judgments, mechanic's liens.
Specific lienAttaching to a particular property.
General lienAttaching to all of the debtor's property in the jurisdiction, including property acquired later while effective.
ReconveyanceThe recorded document clearing a satisfied deed of trust. Payment of the debt does not clear the record — a document does.
Property tax lien priorityGenerally takes priority regardless of when it attached. The principal exception to first-in-time.
Special assessmentA levy for improvements benefiting particular property. Involuntary, specific, and inherited by the buyer.
Mechanic's lienSecuring payment for labor or materials improving real property. Priority may relate back to when work commenced, and rights can arise for parties the owner never dealt with.
Judgment lienA money judgment made a lien on the debtor's real property in a county by recording an abstract. Involuntary and general.
Lis pendensA recorded notice of pending litigation affecting title. Not a lien, and a powerful cloud.
Homestead exemptionProtection of a portion of a homeowner's equity from certain creditors. Does not protect against voluntary liens the owner granted or against tax liens. Effect is a legal question.
EasementA non-possessory right to use another's land for a specified purpose. Runs with the land.
Dominant tenementThe parcel benefited by an easement appurtenant.
Servient tenementThe parcel burdened — it serves the other.
Easement appurtenantBenefits a parcel and passes with it automatically on transfer.
Easement in grossBenefits a person or entity rather than a parcel — a utility line easement.
Easement by necessityArising where a parcel would otherwise be landlocked by the division that created it.
Easement by prescriptionArising from long use meeting the legal requirements. A doctrine to recognize and refer.
LicenseRevocable permission to use another's land, creating no interest and not running with the land.
Non-useGenerally does not terminate an easement.
Private restrictions (CC&Rs)Recorded limits on use binding successive owners. Neither overrides zoning nor is overridden by it — the more restrictive generally governs.
EncroachmentAn improvement extending onto another's land. Disclose, recommend a survey, refer — never characterize.
Constructive noticeKnowledge the law charges a person with because a document was recorded.
Inquiry noticeKnowledge charged from facts that would prompt investigation — an occupant who is not the record owner, a worn path across the lot.
First in time, first in rightThe general priority rule, measured by recording.
Subordination agreementA lienholder's agreement to take a lower position than it would otherwise hold. A significant decision for counsel, not a formality.
Preliminary reportA report of record title stating the terms on which a policy would issue. Not a guarantee, not the policy, not a survey.
ExceptionAn item the policy will not insure against. The buyer bears that risk unless otherwise addressed.
ExclusionA category the policy form does not cover at all — governmental regulation, eminent domain, matters created by the insured.
RequirementSomething the insurer needs before issuing. The items with deadlines attached.

Practice problems

Problem 1

Classify each on both axes and state one practical consequence of the classification: (a) a deed of trust; (b) a property tax lien; (c) a judgment lien; (d) a mechanic's lien.

Answer.

Solution. (a) Voluntary and specific. Created by the owner's agreement and attached to this property. Consequence: it can be sold subject to, or paid from proceeds at closing — which is why the payoff demand, including accrued interest, is obtained rather than assumed from the balance.

(b) Involuntary and specific. Consequence: it generally takes priority regardless of when it attached, which is the principal exception to first-in-time and exists because the taxing power does not depend on the order private parties recorded.

(c) Involuntary and general. Consequence: it reaches every parcel the debtor owns in the county, including property acquired later while the lien is effective — which is why a buyer with an outstanding judgment discovers it attaching to the property he is buying, and why a judgment against a similarly named person must be resolved through title rather than assumed away.

(d) Involuntary and specific. Consequence: its priority may relate back to when work commenced, so it can outrank instruments recorded before it.

Problem 2

A seller renovated the kitchen and rebuilt the deck last spring. He is in an unresolved dispute with the general contractor over the final $18,000, and says two subcontractors he never met have been calling. The preliminary report is clean.

What is the exposure, and what does the licensee do?

Solution. A clean report is a snapshot, not a forecast. Mechanic's lien exposure is exactly what a current report can fail to show.

Two features make this dangerous. Priority may relate back to when work commenced, so a lien recorded next month can outrank a deed of trust recorded before it — which is why lenders care about recent construction. And lien rights arise from work, not from a contract with the owner: the subcontractors and suppliers the seller never dealt with can have rights of their own.

What the licensee does: ask the intake question — has any work been done recently, by whom, and is everyone paid? — route it to escrow, title, and counsel immediately, and ensure it is addressed before the contingency expires.

What the licensee does not do: advise whether a lien would be valid or timely, or reassure the buyer that the dispute is between the seller and his contractor. The statutory scheme's notices and deadlines are legal questions.

Problem 3

A preliminary report shows a ten-foot utility easement along the rear property line. The buyer is purchasing the lot specifically to build a workshop at the rear. The agent tells him easements are routine, offers to ask title to remove it, and says the workshop should be fine.

Assess all three responses.

Solution. All three are wrong, and the third is the one the buyer will rely on.

"Routine" is not an analysis. Most properties have easements; this one may prevent exactly the structure the buyer is buying the property to build.

Title cannot "remove" an exception, and asking misunderstands what an exception is: an item the policy will not insure against. It is not a blemish the insurer chose to note.

Predicting the effect on his plans is outside the license, and it is a legal and land-use question at once.

What the licensee does: obtain the underlying recorded document — width, location, permitted use, maintenance obligations — ensure the buyer reviews it, and route the effect on his plans to counsel and to the jurisdiction before the contingency expires. The exception names the easement; only the document says where it runs.

Problem 4

A neighbor has parked in the seller's driveway for eleven years with permission. The seller says he can revoke it any time. The buyer's agent says eleven years means the neighbor now has an easement. Separately, an old access road across the property has not been used in twenty years, and the seller says it is therefore gone.

Assess each statement.

Solution. Three statements, and all three are conclusions a licensee must not deliver.

The permission is, in the ordinary case, a license — revocable permission creating no interest in the land and not running with it. So far the seller's description is the usual one.

But "eleven years" raises a prescriptive claim, which is a legal doctrine with requirements neither agent can evaluate — and permission itself bears on the analysis. Neither "it's just a license" nor "he has an easement now" is a statement a licensee can make.

Non-use alone generally does not terminate an easement. Easements end by express release, merger, expiration of a stated term, abandonment where the requirements are met, or impossibility of purpose — not by twenty years of nobody driving on it.

What transfers: "we've always let them" and "nobody has used it in years" are both sentences a licensee routes rather than resolves. Disclose the facts, obtain the documents, and refer.

Problem 5

A buyer wants to add a second dwelling unit. The city's zoning permits it. The recorded CC&Rs prohibit more than one dwelling per lot. The agent tells him he is "zoned for it, so you're fine," and adds that the restriction is probably unenforceable because nobody has enforced it in years.

Correct both.

Solution. Zoning permission answers half the question. Private restrictions and zoning come from different sources, are enforced by different parties, and are changed by different procedures — and neither overrides the other. In practice the more restrictive governs: zoning permitting a duplex does not authorize one where the recorded restrictions prohibit it. The buyer must satisfy both.

The enforceability opinion is a legal conclusion the licensee cannot give, and it is the kind a buyer will spend money relying on. Restrictions are enforced by those entitled to enforce them — other owners in the scheme, or the association — and non-enforcement history is a legal argument, not a fact the licensee can assert.

The correct answer: "There are two separate questions — what the city allows and what the recorded restrictions allow, and you have to satisfy both. Here are the CC&Rs; the use article starts on page eleven. The city's planning counter answers the zoning half. Get both answers before your contingency expires, and I'll note that we discussed it."

Problem 6

A buyer notices a well-worn path crossing the rear of the lot and an occupant in the guest house who is not the seller. The seller says the occupant is "just a friend staying temporarily" and there is nothing recorded about the path.

What kind of notice is in play, and what should happen?

Solution. Inquiry notice — the one that surprises people, because nothing was recorded.

The recording system answers who has notice of what. Actual notice is knowing in fact. Constructive notice is what the law charges a person with because a document was recorded — a recorded document is knowable by anyone who looks, so everyone is treated as knowing it. Inquiry notice arises from facts that would prompt a reasonable person to investigate.

An occupant who is not the record owner and a worn path across the lot are the textbook facts. The buyer may be charged with what a reasonable investigation would have revealed, recorded or not — which could include an unrecorded lease, a claimed prescriptive right, or an occupancy the seller cannot terminate on schedule.

What should happen: the facts are disclosed and investigated rather than explained away. Ask for any written agreement with the occupant, route the path to a survey and to counsel, and do not accept "just a friend" as a description of a possessory interest.

Problem 7

A seller carrying financing on a parcel is asked to sign a subordination agreement so a construction lender can record in first position. His agent tells him it is standard and to go ahead. Separately, the buyer declines an owner's title policy because "the lender is getting a title policy anyway."

Assess both.

Solution. Subordination is a significant decision, not a formality. The seller is agreeing to take a lower position than he would otherwise hold, behind a construction loan — and priority determines who is paid first from a limited fund and whose interest survives a foreclosure. A junior lienholder wiped out by a senior foreclosure has lost its security whatever the merits of the debt. Whether to sign belongs to counsel, and "it's standard" is the single most expensive sentence a licensee can say about it.

The owner's and lender's policies insure different interests. The lender's policy insures the lender's lien and its priority — not the buyer's ownership. A buyer who declines an owner's policy has not economized on a duplicate; he has left his own interest uninsured.

Worth adding while the subject is open: extended coverage may address matters a standard policy excepts, including some survey matters, typically requiring a survey or other evidence. Whether to obtain it is the buyer's decision, made informed.

Problem 8

A preliminary report received on day twelve of a fourteen-day review shows: recorded CC&Rs; an unreleased deed of trust the seller says was paid in 2016; a judgment against a person with a name similar to the seller's; a lis pendens; and a requirement for a corporate resolution.

Handle each, and state what went wrong before any of it.

Solution. The timing failure came first, and it is the one that made everything else harder. The preliminary report and its underlying documents belong at the front of the queue with the association documents and hazard-area insurance quotes. An exception discovered on day twelve — an unreleased lien needing a document from a lender that may no longer exist — leaves a formality where a review should have been.

The CC&Rs: obtain and review; they bind the buyer regardless of zoning.

The unreleased deed of trust: a recorded reconveyance must be obtained. Payment of the debt does not clear the record; a document does, and the seller's recollection is not that document.

The similar-name judgment: route to title for resolution. Do not assume it is or is not the seller — a judgment lien is general and reaches everything the debtor owns in the county.

The lis pendens: recognize it as a serious cloud. It is not itself a lien, but it gives notice that pending litigation may affect anyone acquiring an interest, which in practice stops transactions. Route to counsel immediately.

The resolution: this is a requirement, not an exception — something the insurer needs before issuing, and therefore the item with a deadline attached. Distinguish the three throughout: exceptions are risks not insured, exclusions are categories outside the policy, and requirements must be satisfied before closing.

Chapter summary

An encumbrance affects title or use. Liens secure debts; easements, restrictions, and encroachments govern what may be done.

Classify liens on two axes — voluntary or involuntary, general or specific — and read the practical consequence off the classification.

A lien does not prevent a sale; it is ordinarily paid from proceeds, which is why payoff figures exceed principal balances.

Payment does not clear the record. A recorded reconveyance does.

Property tax liens generally take priority regardless of timing, and mechanic's lien priority may relate back — the two exceptions that defeat the first-recorded intuition. Recent construction is an intake question.

An easement is a non-possessory right that runs with the land. The servient parcel serves the dominant one; appurtenant easements pass with the dominant parcel automatically. Non-use generally does not terminate one, and long permitted use is a doctrine to route rather than resolve.

A license is revocable, creates no interest, and does not run with the land — but "we've always let them" belongs to counsel.

Zoning and recorded restrictions are independent, and the more restrictive governs. "Zoned for it, so you're fine" answers half the question, and enforceability is never the licensee's call.

Encroachments are disclosed, surveyed, and referred — never characterized.

Recording answers who has notice. Constructive notice comes from the record; inquiry notice comes from facts on the ground that would prompt investigation.

Priority determines who is paid first and whose interest survives foreclosure, which is why subordination is a decision for counsel rather than a standard formality.

An exception is a risk the policy will not insure against. Read exceptions, obtain the underlying documents, distinguish exceptions from exclusions and requirements, and never treat an item as routine, ask for its removal, or predict its effect.

Order the report early. Late discovery converts a review into a formality.

Required applied assignment

Prepare a one-page file memorandum for the applied scenario presented with this assignment. Classify each encumbrance on both axes, state how each arose and what would remove it, identify the priority questions and any exception to first-in-time that applies, distinguish the exceptions from the exclusions and requirements on the report given, state what you would obtain and in what order and by what deadline, identify what you would route to title, to a surveyor, and to counsel, and state what you would decline to characterize and why. The instructor version contains the scoring rubric.

Knowledge check and remediation

Complete the five-item lesson quiz in the secure learning platform. The lesson mastery threshold is 80 percent — four of the five items. An unsuccessful attempt opens targeted remediation: an alternate explanation of the concepts, a second worked scenario, and a different five-item set covering the same concepts. The 80 percent threshold is a StateCourse instructional policy proposed for DRE review; it is not represented as a DRE-mandated score.

Assignment completion

Completion requires all six instructional segments, the applied memorandum, the quiz submission, and any triggered remediation. Assignment completion does not waive the separate final examination, minimum elapsed-time, identity, proctor, or approval requirements.

Assessment materials for this assignment

These are the assessment items the student is served inside this assignment. In the course itself the student sees only the question and the answer choices — the correct answer and the explanation are withheld until the item has been answered, and the explanation for a failed engagement check is withheld while the student works the remediation set. They are printed here in full because this volume is submitted for review, and a reviewer is entitled to the item, the key and the reasoning.

Applied exercise — 100% required to complete the assignment

1. A preliminary report on a home shows: a first deed of trust, a recorded easement giving the neighbor access across the driveway, a mechanic's lien recorded last month by a roofing contractor, and recorded covenants limiting the property to residential use. The buyer plans to run a small business from a converted garage. Which items most directly threaten his plan and his title?

  1. A. The covenants threaten the intended use, and the mechanic's lien threatens clear title at closing; the easement affects the driveway but not the business use, and the deed of trust is expected to be paid through escrow.
  2. B. All four are equal problems that must be removed before the buyer can close.
  3. C. Only the mechanic's lien matters, because the other three are ordinary and appear on most properties.
  4. D. Only the easement matters, because it gives a third party rights in the property the buyer is purchasing.

Answer: A. Encumbrances have to be read for what each one does. Private use restrictions are what defeat a business use; an unresolved mechanic's lien is a money encumbrance that must be cleared or insured over; an access easement burdens the driveway; and the seller's financing is routinely paid off through escrow.

Engagement check — 5 items, 80% required

1. What distinguishes a voluntary lien from an involuntary lien?

  1. A. A voluntary lien is created by the owner's own act, such as a deed of trust; an involuntary lien arises by operation of law, such as a tax or judgment lien.
  2. B. A voluntary lien may be removed at the owner's discretion; an involuntary lien may not.
  3. C. A voluntary lien is recorded while an involuntary lien is not.
  4. D. A voluntary lien secures a debt while an involuntary lien does not.

Answer: A. The distinction is how the lien came into existence — by the owner's act or by law. Both are typically recorded, both can secure obligations, and neither is removable at will.

2. What is the difference between an easement and a license?

  1. A. An easement is an interest in land that generally runs with the property; a license is a personal privilege that is generally revocable.
  2. B. An easement is temporary while a license is permanent.
  3. C. An easement benefits the owner of the land while a license benefits a third party.
  4. D. An easement must be paid for while a license is granted without consideration.

Answer: A. Durability and the nature of the interest separate them: an easement is a property interest that survives transfer, while a license is permission that can ordinarily be withdrawn.

3. In an easement appurtenant, what are the dominant and servient tenements?

  1. A. The dominant tenement is the parcel benefited by the easement; the servient tenement is the parcel burdened by it.
  2. B. The dominant tenement is the larger parcel; the servient tenement is the smaller one.
  3. C. The dominant tenement is the parcel that was created first; the servient tenement was created later.
  4. D. The dominant tenement is the parcel that pays for maintenance; the servient tenement uses it.

Answer: A. Benefit and burden define the two parcels. Size, order of creation, and maintenance responsibility do not.

4. How is priority among recorded liens generally determined?

  1. A. Generally by the order of recording, first in time being first in right, with certain liens such as property tax liens given priority regardless of when they were recorded.
  2. B. Strictly by the order in which the underlying debts were incurred.
  3. C. By the size of each lien, with larger liens taking priority.
  4. D. By agreement among the lienholders, without which no priority exists.

Answer: A. Recording order is the general rule with statutory exceptions, most notably property taxes. The date the debt arose, the amount, and private agreement do not set the general rule — though lienholders can subordinate by agreement.

5. What is the practical effect of recorded covenants and restrictions on a parcel?

  1. A. They are private restrictions that bind successive owners and limit use independently of what zoning permits.
  2. B. They are enforceable only against the original parties who agreed to them.
  3. C. They override zoning where the two conflict, because they are recorded against the specific property.
  4. D. They expire automatically when the property is sold to a new owner.

Answer: A. Recorded restrictions run with the land and bind later owners. They operate alongside zoning rather than overriding it, and in practice the more restrictive of the two governs what the owner may actually do.

Remediation set — served only after a failed engagement check

1. A property owner has used a path across a neighbor's land for many years without permission. What issue does this raise?

  1. A. A possible prescriptive easement claim, which is a legal question requiring counsel rather than a determination a licensee can make.
  2. B. An automatic easement, since long use establishes the right.
  3. C. No issue, because use without permission cannot create rights.
  4. D. A license, which the neighbor may revoke at any time without consequence.

Answer: A. Long adverse use may ripen into a right, but whether it has depends on legal elements a licensee is not qualified to evaluate. Neither the automatic-right answer nor the no-rights-ever answer is correct.

2. A contractor records a mechanic's lien for unpaid work. What makes this lien distinctive in priority terms?

  1. A. Its priority may relate back to when the work or improvement commenced rather than to the date the lien was recorded.
  2. B. It always takes priority over every other lien on the property.
  3. C. It takes priority only over liens recorded after the contractor completed the work.
  4. D. It has no priority until the contractor obtains a judgment.

Answer: A. The relation-back feature is what makes mechanic's liens a hazard for lenders and buyers: a lien recorded later can outrank an interest that attached after the work began. It measures the lien from commencement rather than promoting it to first position, so it does not reach an encumbrance already attached and of record when work started. It is neither automatically first nor dependent on a judgment.

3. A buyer's preliminary report lists a utility easement running along the rear property line. What should the licensee advise?

  1. A. Review the recorded document to see the easement's width, location, and permitted use before assuming it will not affect the buyer's plans.
  2. B. Disregard it, since utility easements are standard on nearly all properties.
  3. C. Ask the title company to except it from the report.
  4. D. Advise the buyer that the utility must obtain permission before entering the easement area.

Answer: A. The recorded document is what defines the burden, and a rear-line utility easement can prevent structures the buyer intends to build. Commonness is not analysis, exceptions are not removed on request, and the easement holder does not need fresh permission to use its rights.

4. What does it mean that a title insurance policy 'excepts' an item shown in the preliminary report?

  1. A. The policy does not insure against loss arising from that item, so the buyer bears that risk unless it is otherwise addressed.
  2. B. The item has been removed from title as a condition of issuing the policy.
  3. C. The insurer will defend a claim on that item but will not pay a loss.
  4. D. The item is insured only up to the amount of the buyer's down payment.

Answer: A. An exception carves the item out of coverage, which is why exceptions must be read rather than skimmed. It does not clear the item from title and it is not a partial or defense-only coverage.

5. Zoning permits a duplex on a parcel, but the recorded covenants limit it to a single-family residence. What may the owner build?

  1. A. A single-family residence, because the private restriction is more restrictive and both apply.
  2. B. A duplex, because public zoning supersedes private restrictions.
  3. C. A duplex, because covenants apply only until the subdivision is fully built out.
  4. D. Either, at the owner's election, since the two authorities conflict.

Answer: A. Both apply simultaneously, so the owner must satisfy each — which means the stricter one controls the outcome. Zoning permits rather than compels, so it does not override a private restriction.

Real Estate Principles - Lesson Assignment 06

Government powers, land use, and environmental controls

Course version: 1.0 submission draft Assignment time: 180 instructional minutes Regulatory status: Not approved; no California credit is available.

Learning objectives

  • Identify the four government powers over private property and distinguish them by what each takes and what compensation each requires.
  • Explain how a general plan, zoning, and the entitlement process relate, and identify what each answers.
  • Describe subdivision and building controls and explain what a permit record does and does not establish.
  • Identify the environmental hazards a California residential transaction commonly raises and state the licensee's role for each.
  • Explain natural hazard disclosure and water-related requirements at the level a licensee must handle them.
  • Build a land-use due diligence sequence that puts slow items first.

Timed sequence

ActivityMinutesEvidence
Guided reading: government powers and the planning framework55Sections 1-2 viewed and notes saved
Guided reading: subdivision, building controls, and environmental hazards50Sections 3-4 viewed
Guided reading: natural hazard context and due diligence45Sections 5-6 viewed
Applied scenario and decision memorandum20Written response submitted
Lesson assessment10Five scored items submitted
Total180One of 15 separate lesson assignments

1. Taxation, eminent domain, police power, and escheat

1.1 Fee simple absolute is not absolute against government

Lesson 03 established that fee simple absolute is the greatest estate the law recognizes. It is nonetheless subject to four government powers, conventionally remembered as PETE:

PowerWhat it doesCompensation
P — Police powerRegulates use for public health, safety, morals, and general welfareNone
E — Eminent domainTakes property for public useJust compensation required
T — TaxationLevies on property to fund governmentNone; it is a charge, not a taking
E — EscheatProperty passes to the state where an owner dies with no heirs and no willNone

The compensation column is the distinction that matters. Regulation under the police power reduces what an owner may do without paying him; eminent domain takes and pays.

1.2 Police power

The broadest of the four, and the source of zoning, building codes, subdivision regulation, environmental controls, health and safety requirements, and rent regulation where a jurisdiction has adopted it.

The power is exercised by state and local government. Its exercise must serve a legitimate public purpose and must not be arbitrary — but within those limits it can substantially reduce what an owner may do, and the owner is not compensated.

A parcel zoned for commercial use is rezoned residential, and its market value falls by half. That is regulation, not a taking, in the ordinary case. The owner has not lost the property; he has lost uses.

Where regulation goes so far as to deprive an owner of substantially all economically beneficial use, the question of a regulatory taking arises. Whether a particular regulation crosses that line is a legal question of real complexity, and a licensee's role is to recognize the concept, never to advise that a client has a claim.

1.3 Eminent domain

The power to take private property for public use upon payment of just compensation. The process is called condemnation.

Two situations a licensee should be able to name:

Partial taking. Where only part of a parcel is taken, compensation may address both the part taken and severance damages to what remains — for example, where the remainder is left an unusable shape or loses its access.

Inverse condemnation. Where government action effectively takes or damages property without a formal proceeding, and the owner brings the claim rather than the government.

A pending or threatened condemnation is a material fact. It affects value, marketability, and the buyer's plans, and it is disclosed. Whether the owner has a claim, what compensation is due, and how to respond are legal questions for counsel.

1.4 Taxation

Property taxation is taken up in Lesson 13. For present purposes:

  • Property taxes become a lien on the property, generally with priority over other liens regardless of when they attached.
  • Special assessments fund improvements benefiting particular property, and a buyer inherits the remaining obligation.
  • Unpaid property taxes can ultimately lead to sale of the property under the applicable process.

1.5 Escheat

Where a person dies owning property with no will and no heirs who take under the law of intestate succession, the property passes to the state. It is uncommon in residential practice and appears mainly as a concept and occasionally in a chain of title.

1.6 What a licensee actually does with this section

Three things:

  1. Recognize which power is operating. A rezoning is police power; a road widening that takes twelve feet of frontage is eminent domain.
  2. Treat pending government action as a material fact — a proposed rezoning, an announced project, a pending condemnation.
  3. Refer the legal questions. Whether compensation is owed, whether a regulation has gone too far, and what a taking is worth are all outside the license.

1.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to name the four powers, state which requires compensation, and distinguish regulation from a taking on a set of facts.

2. Zoning and general plans

2.1 The planning hierarchy

California land use is organized in layers, and each answers a different question.

LayerQuestion it answers
General planWhat does this jurisdiction intend this area to become?
Specific planHow will that intent be implemented in this particular area?
Zoning ordinanceWhat uses and development standards apply to this parcel now?
Entitlements and permitsWhat has this particular parcel actually been approved for?

The general plan is the long-range policy document, and California requires local general plans to address specified elements — land use, circulation, housing, conservation, open space, noise, and safety among them. Zoning is generally required to be consistent with the general plan.

For a licensee the operative point is that the general plan describes intent while zoning controls today, and a buyer asking "will this area change?" is asking a general plan question, answered by the jurisdiction rather than by the licensee.

2.2 What a zoning ordinance controls

Use — what may occur on the parcel: residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, mixed, and the subcategories within each.

Development standards — the physical envelope: setbacks from each property line, maximum height, lot coverage, floor area ratio, minimum lot size, parking requirements, and open space.

Both halves matter. A parcel zoned to permit a second unit may still be unable to accommodate one within the setbacks, the height limit, and the parking requirement. Permitted use and physical feasibility are different questions, and clients routinely conflate them.

2.3 The relief mechanisms

Where a proposal does not fit the ordinance, three mechanisms are commonly available, and they are frequently confused.

MechanismWhat it addresses
VarianceRelief from a development standard — a setback, a height limit — usually requiring a hardship arising from the property itself
Conditional use permitPermission for a use the ordinance allows in that zone subject to review and conditions
RezoningA change to the ordinance itself, moving the parcel to a different zone

The distinction to hold: a variance addresses the envelope; a conditional use permit addresses the use; a rezoning changes the rule.

All three are discretionary. Nobody is entitled to one, and a licensee who tells a buyer a variance "won't be a problem" has predicted a discretionary decision — which Lesson 13 of the Practice course identifies as a prediction stated as certainty.

2.4 Nonconforming use

A legal nonconforming use is one that was lawful when established and no longer conforms because the ordinance changed. It is commonly permitted to continue — often described as being "grandfathered."

Three limits that surprise owners:

  • Expansion is generally restricted. The right is usually to continue, not to enlarge.
  • Discontinuance can end it. Many ordinances terminate the right after a period of abandonment.
  • Destruction can end it. Rebuilding after substantial destruction may not be permitted.

And a use that was never lawful is not a nonconforming use. It is an unpermitted use, which is a different and worse problem — and "it's been like that for thirty years" does not convert one into the other.

2.5 Recorded restrictions again

From Lesson 05, restated because it belongs here too: zoning and recorded private restrictions are independent, and the more restrictive generally governs in practice. Zoning permitting a use does not authorize it where the CC&Rs prohibit it. A buyer must satisfy both.

2.6 What a licensee may say

May: identify the current zoning designation with its source; explain that zoning governs use and development standards; explain that variances, conditional use permits, and rezonings exist and are discretionary; direct the buyer to the planning counter; and confirm that the buyer investigated before his contingency expired.

May not: state that a use is permitted; predict that an application will be approved; interpret setback or height provisions for the buyer's project; or characterize an existing condition as legally nonconforming.

A buyer asks: "Can I build a second unit here?"

Correct: "That's two questions — what the zoning allows and whether the lot can physically fit it within setbacks, height, and parking, plus whatever the recorded restrictions say. The city's planning counter answers the first two, and I'll get you the CC&Rs for the third. Let's get both before your contingency expires, and I'll note we discussed it."

Incorrect: "The zoning allows it, so you're fine."

2.7 A worked land-use inquiry

A buyer under contract on a residence tells the licensee he intends to convert the detached garage into a rental unit, run a small contracting business from the property, and add a second story.

Three plans, and each is governed by more than one system.

The public side — Section 2.2's ordinance. Whether the zone permits an accessory dwelling unit, what standards apply to it, whether a home occupation is permitted and on what conditions, and what height, setback, and coverage limits apply to a second story. Each has an answer, and the answers come from the jurisdiction rather than from the licensee.

The relief mechanisms — Section 2.3. Where the ordinance does not permit something as of right, a variance or a conditional use permit may exist as a path. They are processes with standards, timelines, hearings, and no guaranteed outcome, and "you can just get a variance" is one of the more damaging sentences a licensee can say.

The private side — Section 2.5 and Lesson 05, Section 4.2. Recorded restrictions can prohibit what zoning permits. A property in a development whose declaration forbids rentals or business use is a property where the zoning answer is irrelevant to the buyer's plan.

The building side — Section 3.2. Permits, plans, and inspections, and a conversion of existing space carries its own requirements. Section 3.3's unpermitted-work problem is what this becomes if the buyer proceeds without them.

The practical sequence the licensee recommends, in writing:

  1. Ask the jurisdiction — planning for use and standards, building for permit requirements — before removing contingencies.
  2. Obtain and read the recorded restrictions, and route their interpretation to counsel.
  3. Confirm with a design or construction professional what the existing structure will actually support.
  4. Confirm insurance and financing implications where a use changes.

What the licensee says, and what he does not.

He says: these are three separate questions with four sources of answers, here is where each answer comes from, and here is the deadline by which you need them.

He does not say: "ADUs are allowed everywhere now," "nobody enforces the home-occupation rules," "you can add a second story, the neighbor did," or any version of what the ordinance permits. Section 2.6 states the boundary, and the neighbor's second story is the least reliable evidence available — it may have been permitted under a different ordinance, granted relief, or built without permission.

The recurring error this prevents. A buyer removes his contingencies on the strength of a licensee's encouragement, closes, and discovers that the conversion he bought the property for requires a discretionary approval he will not get. The information was available on day two, from a phone call to a public counter, and the licensee's contribution was to say who to call.

2.8 Checkpoint

You should be able to distinguish a variance from a conditional use permit, explain the limits on a nonconforming use, and answer a buildability question correctly.

3. Subdivision and building controls

3.1 The two subdivision statutes, revisited

From Lesson 04, because it is the land use half that matters here:

The Subdivision Map Act governs the creation of parcels — the tentative and final map process, the conditions a local agency may impose, dedications, and required improvements. It answers whether a parcel may lawfully be created and sold.

The Subdivided Lands Law is the DRE-administered consumer protection statute governing the sale of subdivided interests, including the public report requirement before certain subdivided property may be offered.

The recurring practice point: a separate tax bill is not evidence of a lawful split. Where a parcel's creation is in question, it goes to the local agency, to title, and to counsel — before it is marketed as a separate building site, because marketing it as one is a factual claim about entitlement.

3.2 Building codes and permits

Building codes set minimum standards for construction, and work generally requires a permit and inspections culminating in a final approval.

What a permit record establishes and does not:

EstablishesDoes not establish
That a permit was issued for described workThat the work was completed
That inspections were performed, where finaledThat the work was done well
The scope as permittedThat subsequent work was permitted
A dateThat current condition matches the permit

A permit that was issued but never finaled is a real problem — an open permit can complicate a sale, and the obligation to close it out generally follows the property.

3.3 Unpermitted work

This is among the most common problems in California residential transactions, and licensees mishandle it in both directions.

The facts to establish: what work was done, when, whether a permit was issued, whether it was finaled, and whether the work is habitable and safe as built.

What the licensee does:

  1. Disclose what is known, including what the seller said and what the licensee observed.
  2. Recommend permit research at the jurisdiction — which is a public record and is where the answer actually lives.
  3. Do not include unpermitted area in advertised square footage without disclosing its status.
  4. Recommend the buyer investigate what legalization would require, since the cost can be substantial and sometimes the work cannot be legalized at all.
  5. Document the recommendation and the buyer's response.

What the licensee does not do: state that the work is legal because it looks fine, characterize the risk as low, predict what the city would require, or advise the seller to say nothing because "everyone does it."

The asymmetry worth teaching: unpermitted work does not automatically make a property unsaleable, and it does automatically make it a disclosure item. Licensees fail on both sides — some conceal it, some describe it as a disaster. The professional response is to make it visible and investigable.

3.4 Certificates and clearances

Depending on the jurisdiction and the property type, a transfer may trigger local requirements — retrofit obligations for smoke and carbon monoxide devices and water conservation fixtures, occupancy or resale inspections, sewer lateral requirements, or point-of-sale reports.

These are local and they vary. A licensee working across city lines who assumes uniformity will eventually miss one, and a missed point-of-sale requirement can delay a closing.

3.5 Accessibility in new construction

Certain multifamily housing is subject to accessible design and construction requirements, and California standards can exceed the federal baseline. A licensee marketing new construction should not represent that a property meets accessibility requirements without confirming it, and should direct specific questions to the developer, the architect, or the jurisdiction.

3.7 Two subdivision statutes, and why California has both

Section 3.1 described subdivision approval as a local process. It is that, and it is also a state one, and the two run on different definitions. A licensee who knows only "five or more parcels" has half of it.

The Subdivision Map Act — Government Code § 66410 and following. The Act names itself in a single sentence: "This division may be cited as the Subdivision Map Act." It is the local land-division statute: it governs how land is divided, what maps are filed, and what conditions a city or county may impose.

Its definition, at Government Code § 66424, is deliberately broad:

"…any unimproved land, or any portion thereof, shown on the latest equalized county assessment roll as a unit or as contiguous units, for the purpose of sale, lease, or financing, whether immediate or future. Property shall be considered as contiguous units, even if it is separated by roads, streets, utility easement, or railroad rights-of-way. 'Subdivision' includes a condominium project …, a community apartment project …, or the conversion of five or more existing dwelling units to a stock cooperative…"

The Subdivided Lands Act — Business and Professions Code § 11000 and following. This is the consumer-protection statute, administered by the Department of Real Estate, and it is why a public report exists. Its definition is narrower and counts differently:

"'Subdivided lands' and 'subdivision' refer to improved or unimproved land or lands, wherever situated within California, divided or proposed to be divided for the purpose of sale or lease or financing, whether immediate or future, into five or more lots or parcels."

The two acts do not overlap neatly, and that is the point.

Subdivision Map ActSubdivided Lands Act
CodeGov. Code § 66410 et seq.B&P Code § 11000 et seq.
Administered byCities and countiesThe Department of Real Estate
PurposeHow land may be divided; maps, conditions, dedicationsWhether the offering may be sold to the public; disclosure
TriggerDivision of land into parcels, including twoFive or more lots or parcels
OutputTentative and final maps; parcel mapsPublic report

Three consequences worth carrying.

A two-lot split is a subdivision for map purposes and not for public-report purposes. The owner deals with the county and files a parcel map; no DRE public report is involved. A licensee who tells such an owner they need a public report is wrong, and one who tells a five-lot subdivider they do not is wrong more expensively.

"Contiguous even if separated by roads" closes an obvious avoidance route. An owner cannot escape the Map Act by pointing at the street between their two holdings.

A condominium project is a subdivision. § 66424 says so expressly. Converting an apartment building to condominiums is a land division in the eyes of the Map Act even though no soil is moved, and converting five or more units to a stock cooperative is too. The most common "subdivision" a residential licensee will ever touch involves no vacant land at all.

3.8 The 160-acre carve-out and the exclusions

§ 11000 carries exclusions that show what the Legislature was aiming at.

The 160-acre parcels. Land "sold by lots or parcels of not less than 160 acres which are designated by lot or parcel description by government surveys and appear as such on the current assessment roll" is not subdivided land — unless it is divided for sale for oil and gas purposes, in which case it is. The consumer-protection concern was never large agricultural parcels described by government survey; it was the sale of small parcels to buyers who cannot inspect what they are buying. But oil and gas is carved back in, because that is a pattern the Legislature had specific reason to reach.

Ordinary leasing is out. The chapter "does not apply to the leasing of apartments, offices, stores, or similar space within an apartment building, industrial building, commercial building, or mobilehome park." Renting an office suite is not subdividing.

With two exceptions that are back in. Mobile home park leases "for a term in excess of five years … as a mandatory requirement and prerequisite to tenancy" are subject to the chapter. And leasing apartments in a community apartment project is subject to it. Both are situations where a "lease" is functionally the sale of a long-term interest to a consumer.
