What forfeits a contingency's protection: notifying the other agent verbally, instructing escrow unilaterally to return the deposit, or simply ceasing to perform and letting the other party cancel for non-performance — which is a materially worse position.

6.8 What actually prevents disputes

Most transaction disputes are not about substance. They are about whether something was delivered, to whom, and when — which is why the practices that prevent them are documentary:

  1. Build the deadline calendar from the contract and share it in writing.
  2. Deliver notices by the authorized method and keep the evidence.
  3. Confirm materially important conversations in writing.
  4. Amend in writing, signed, and deliver to escrow.
  5. Correct errors immediately, in writing, to everyone who received the original.
  6. Keep superseded drafts, so the sequence of versions shows how terms changed.
  7. Audit the file at closing while memories are fresh.

6.9 The contract questions a licensee must route

This lesson describes contract law because a licensee works with contracts daily. It does not qualify him to answer questions about them, and the boundary is harder here than anywhere else in the course, because the questions arrive constantly and they sound like transaction questions.

The questionWhy it routes
"Is this contract still enforceable?"Enforceability is the legal conclusion, and it depends on facts and law rather than on the document's appearance
"Did they breach?"A legal characterization with consequences attached to it
"Can I cancel and get my deposit back?"Two legal questions — the right to cancel and the disposition of the deposit
"What are my damages?"Section 6.1's territory, and none of it is the licensee's
"Does the liquidated damages clause apply here?"Section 6.4 explains the concept; whether it operates on these facts is counsel's
"Can I sue for specific performance?"Section 6.3 explains why the remedy exists; whether to pursue it is legal advice
"Is this counteroffer still open?"Formation and revocation, applied to facts — the practice course's worked formation problem shows how quickly this gets hard
"Was that email an acceptance?"Same
"Can I add a clause saying they'll pay if the appraisal is low?"Drafting a provision that alters rights. Section 4.1 of Lesson 01
"They signed but wrote a note in the margin — what does that do?"Formation, again, and the answer is genuinely uncertain
"Do I have to disclose that the last deal fell through?"A disclosure question with a legal answer

What the licensee can do with every one of these, and it is substantial:

  1. Explain what the document provides for procedurally — what step comes next, what the deadline is, what the form requires.
  2. Identify that a legal question exists, which is a service most clients cannot perform for themselves.
  3. Recommend counsel in writing, with a date, before the deadline that makes the answer moot.
  4. Preserve the facts — the dates, the communications, the sequence — so that counsel is answering from a record rather than from recollection.
  5. Escalate to the broker, who decides what the brokerage does.

The distinction that makes this workable. "Your contingency period ends Friday at 5" is a fact about the document. "Your contingency protects you if you cancel Friday" is a legal opinion about your rights, and the two sentences are one word apart.

And the reason the boundary is protective rather than restrictive. Section 4.3 of Lesson 01 makes the general point; here it is specific. A licensee who answers a contract question and is wrong has caused a loss he is answerable for, on a subject where he had no authority to speak and where the client had a right to a qualified answer. The referral costs nothing and transfers the question to the person who can answer it.

6.10 What actually goes wrong in formation

The elements in Section 1 and the mechanics in Section 2 describe how a contract forms. Real transactions fail formation in a small number of recognizable ways, and each is prevented by a habit rather than by knowledge.

The failureWhat happenedThe habit that prevents it
Acceptance not communicatedA signature exists; nothing shows it reached the offeror before expirationTransmit and confirm receipt the moment a document is signed
Signed after expirationThe offer lapsed before the signatureCalendar every expiration, on both sides
A counteroffer treated as an acceptanceA term was changed; the original offer is terminated and a new one existsRead what was returned rather than assuming it came back the way it went out
Two documents both signedAn offer and a counteroffer both executed, in an unclear orderOne live document at a time, and the sequence dated
A term left blankFilled in later, by someone, off the pageNever transmit an incomplete document, and never complete one after signature
An oral agreement to change a termSection 4's problem, and the operative document still says the originalSame-day written amendment, without exception
Delivery to the wrong personSent to a party rather than through the agreed channel, or to an address never consented toUse the transmission method the agreement specifies, and evidence it
Signature by someone without authorityA co-owner, a trustee, an entity signatory, or an attorney-in-fact whose authority was assumedLesson 03's intake questions, asked before the offer
A margin noteAn annotation on a signed page that may or may not be a change of termsAnything that changes a term goes in an amendment, not in a margin

Two of these deserve emphasis because they recur most.

Communication of acceptance. Formation turns on it, and licensees consistently treat the signature as the event. A signed acceptance in an outbox has not formed a contract, and the practice course's worked formation problem shows how quickly that fact becomes consequential when circumstances change in the intervening hour.

The incomplete document. A blank in a material term is not a formality. The document the party signed is not the document in the file, and no explanation of good intent survives that fact.

What a licensee should take from this section. Section 6.9 establishes that the legal questions route to counsel. This table is not legal analysis — it is a list of operational habits, and every one of them is performed by the licensee rather than by anyone else in the transaction. The contract questions belong to counsel; the reasons counsel gets called usually belong to the file.

6.11 What a licensee actually does with contract law

This lesson is the longest legal treatment in the course, and its practical yield is smaller and more specific than students expect.

It does not qualify a licensee to advise on contracts. Section 6.9 lists what routes.

What it does is make four things possible.

One: recognizing that a legal question exists. A client asks something that sounds procedural and is not. A licensee who has studied formation, capacity, the Statute of Frauds, and remedies will notice — and noticing is the whole service, because a client who does not know he needs counsel will not call one.

Two: performing the operational work correctly. Section 6.10's table is entirely operational: transmitting, confirming, calendaring, refusing to send an incomplete document, reducing agreements to writing the same day. None of that requires legal judgment and all of it prevents legal problems.

Three: preserving the facts an answer will depend on. When a contract question does arise, its answer turns on dates, sequence, what was communicated, and what each party received. A licensee who has kept that record has given counsel something to work with; one who has not has given counsel four recollections.

Four: explaining the document's own terms without characterizing their effect. "Your contingency period ends Friday at five, and here is what the agreement says the removal has to look like" is a service. "You're protected until Friday" is an opinion about rights. The two sentences are close, and the distance between them is the entire boundary.

The three habits that carry most of the value:

  1. Everything material in writing, the same day.
  2. Every deadline in a system, counted from the event the agreement names rather than from the day everyone remembers.
  3. Every transmission evidenced, because formation and performance both turn on communication rather than on signature.

The test of whether this lesson worked. Not whether a student can recite the elements — but whether, handed a real situation, he can say which parts are his to handle, which parts are counsel's, and what the file needs to show either way. Those three judgments are what the lesson was for, and they are what a first year in practice will ask for repeatedly.

6.13 Damages, specific performance, and liquidated damages compared

Section 6.4 named the remedies. This section sets them against each other, because a client's real question is always "what do I actually get."

RemedyWhat it givesWhen it is realistic
Compensatory damagesMoney to put the injured party where performance would haveWhenever loss can be proved. The usual remedy
Specific performanceA court order to convey the propertyReal property only, in practice — because each parcel is treated as unique, money is presumed inadequate
Liquidated damagesThe agreed sum, without proving actual lossWhere the clause was properly formed and initialled
Rescission and restitutionUnwinding; each party returns what they receivedFraud, mutual mistake, failure of consideration

Specific performance is the remedy that distinguishes real property. A buyer of a car who is refused delivery buys another car and sues for the difference. A buyer of a particular house cannot, because there is no other identical house. The uniqueness of land is not sentiment; it is the doctrinal reason the remedy exists.

Liquidated damages solve a problem that money damages create. A seller whose buyer defaults must otherwise prove what the breach cost — carrying costs, a lower resale price, time on market — which is expensive and uncertain. A liquidated damages clause fixes the number in advance. In California residential purchase agreements the clause is separately initialled, and that separate initialling is not a formality: it is the parties' evidence that they agreed to the substitution rather than absorbing it in the boilerplate.

What a licensee must not do with any of this. Tell a client what they will recover. Every row in that table is a legal conclusion, and each depends on facts a licensee has not verified and doctrines a licensee has not studied.

6.14 A worked breach, four ways

A buyer and seller sign a purchase agreement at $880,000 with a $26,400 deposit and an initialled liquidated damages clause. The buyer removes all contingencies. Two weeks before closing, the buyer's circumstances change and the buyer refuses to close. The seller relists and sells four months later for $845,000, having carried the property at $4,200 a month.

If the seller pursues actual damages. The measurable loss is roughly $35,000 in price plus about $16,800 in carrying costs — call it $51,800 — less anything the seller saved. The seller must prove each element, and the buyer will contest the resale price, the marketing, and whether the carrying costs were avoidable.

If the seller relies on liquidated damages. The seller takes the $26,400 deposit and proves nothing. That is roughly half the arguable loss, and it is available immediately and without litigation.

Which is better is not obvious, and it is exactly the sort of judgment that belongs to the seller with counsel's advice. The licensee's contribution is to make sure the seller understands there is a choice, and to say nothing about which way it should go.

If the buyer sues for return of the deposit, arguing the clause is unenforceable — the analysis turns on how the clause was formed and on statutory limits applicable to residential purchases. A licensee has no view on this.

If the seller had wanted the buyer to complete, specific performance would in principle be available to a seller as well as to a buyer, though it is far less commonly pursued: a seller usually wants money and another buyer, not a decree compelling a reluctant purchaser to take a house.

The single most useful thing a licensee can do in this scenario happens before any of it — making sure the liquidated damages clause was properly initialled at signing. A clause not initialled is a remedy the seller does not have, and discovering that at the moment of breach is discovering it too late.

6.15 Checkpoint

You should be able to name the remedies, explain why specific performance is available for real property, and give the correct answer to a client asking about a deposit.

Key terms

TermDefinition
The four elementsMutual assent, consideration, capacity, and lawful object.
Express / impliedStated in words, or inferred from conduct.
Bilateral / unilateralA promise for a promise, or a promise for an act. A purchase agreement is bilateral; an open listing is unilateral.
Executory / executedSomething remains to be done, or fully performed. "Executed" in classification means performed, not signed.
OfferA proposal showing present intent to be bound, reasonably definite, and communicated. A listing invites offers; it is not one.
Mirror-image acceptanceAn acceptance must match the offer; any change to a material term is not an acceptance.
Communication of acceptanceThe rule most often skipped. A signed acceptance nobody delivered has not been communicated.
CounterofferA rejection of the original offer and the substitution of a new one. The original is gone, not suspended — including where the change is handwritten on a signed form.
RevocationWithdrawal before acceptance, generally permitted even where the offer states a deadline.
OptionA contract making an offer irrevocable for a period, supported by consideration.
ConsiderationValue exchanged. Adequacy is generally not examined; past consideration generally is not consideration; forbearance can be.
CapacityThe legal ability to contract. A licensee's concern is authority, not diagnosis — where capacity is in question, stop, escalate, and refer.
Lawful objectA purpose the law permits. Provisions the law will not enforce fail whether or not both parties agreed.
VoidNo contract exists and never did.
VoidableA valid contract one party may elect to avoid — and may instead affirm.
UnenforceableA contract a court will not enforce, though it may have other effects.
Fraud / negligent misrepresentationA knowing misstatement intended to be relied on; or a statement made without reasonable basis or care. Most claims against licensees are the second.
Statute of FraudsThe requirement that certain contracts be in writing and signed by the party to be charged — including sales of real property, leases over one year, and compensation agreements.
Part performanceA doctrine under which a court may enforce an oral agreement where a party took possession, paid, and improved in reliance.
Written amendmentThe only thing that changes a contract term. Agent emails, verbal agreements, and escrow instructions alone change nothing.
ContingencyA condition on a party's obligation inside a formed contract — not a delay of formation, not a general right to cancel.
Written removalHow contingencies end under the standard California form. A passed date removes nothing; the seller's route is the contractual notice.
AssignmentTransfer of contract rights, with the assignor frequently remaining liable.
NovationSubstitution of a party or contract with all parties' consent, generally releasing the original.
WaiverGiving up a contract right. Removes the contractual path to act, not the ability to investigate.
Material breachA failure going to the essence of the bargain, which may excuse further performance. Whether a breach is material is a legal question.
Specific performanceA court order requiring the promised performance. Available for real property because of uniqueness.
Liquidated damagesAn amount agreed in advance as the recovery on default. Must be properly agreed, is constrained by law, and generally limits rather than adds.
RescissionUnwinding the contract with restoration. Not a synonym for cancellation under a contingency.
CancellationExercising a right the contract provides, by the procedure it specifies. Not accomplished by announcing, ceasing to perform, or instructing escrow.

Practice problems

Problem 1

Classify a residential purchase agreement on all four axes at the moment of acceptance. Then classify an open listing offering compensation to whoever produces a buyer.

Answer.

Solution. The purchase agreement at acceptance: express — stated in words; bilateral — the buyer promises to buy and the seller promises to sell, and both are bound on formation; executory — both still owe performance until closing; and valid, assuming the four elements are present.

It becomes executed at closing, when both have fully performed. The vocabulary trips students because "executed" colloquially means signed — in classification it means fully performed, so a signed but unperformed agreement is executory.

The open listing is unilateral — a promise to pay if someone performs an act. Nobody is bound to perform, and therefore nobody breaches by not performing. An exclusive right to sell listing, by contrast, is bilateral: the brokerage promises to market and the seller promises to pay on the agreed terms.

Problem 2

A buyer offers $880,000, open until 5:00 p.m. Friday. Wednesday, he withdraws it. Thursday, the seller signs it and puts it in his file. Friday morning the seller's agent emails the signed copy.

Was a contract formed?

Solution. No, on two independent grounds — either one is enough.

The offer was revoked before acceptance. An offer may generally be revoked before acceptance even where it states a deadline, unless supported by consideration as an option — which is precisely what an option buys: irrevocability for the period.

And acceptance was not communicated on Thursday. A signed acceptance sitting in a file has not been communicated to the offeror, so nothing formed then; by Friday there was nothing left to accept.

What transfers, in both directions: a buyer relying on "open until Friday" should know it can be withdrawn Wednesday, and a seller intending to accept should not assume the offer will still be there. The communication rule is the one most often skipped — including in signing platforms, where an executed document nobody delivered has not been delivered.

Problem 3

A buyer offers $880,000. The seller strikes the price to $895,000 and the closing date to March 20, signs, and returns it. The buyer signs it but crosses out March 20 and writes March 25 before returning. The seller now says he prefers the original $880,000 offer and will accept it.

Where do the parties stand?

Solution. No contract, and the original offer is gone.

The seller's changes were a counteroffer, which rejected the $880,000 offer and substituted a new one. It was not an "acceptance with modifications" forming a contract on his terms, and it did not suspend the original leaving it available — the original can no longer be accepted unless the buyer renews it.

The buyer's handwritten date change is a further counteroffer, however small. Signing does not convert a modification into an acceptance.

The buyer's counteroffer at $895,000 / March 25 is outstanding. The seller may accept it, reject it, or counter again — or ask the buyer to renew the original terms, which the buyer is free to decline.

Problem 4

Four situations: (a) a seller and buyer agree to conceal a known foundation defect from the lender; (b) a 17-year-old signs a purchase agreement; (c) an oral agreement to sell a house, where the buyer has taken possession, paid $60,000, and rebuilt the kitchen; (d) a lease clause waiving the landlord's habitability obligation.

Classify each as void, voidable, or unenforceable, and state the practical consequence.

Solution. (a) Void. A contract for an unlawful purpose. No contract exists and never did; nobody can enforce it.

(b) Voidable by the minor. This is a valid, binding contract until the minor elects to avoid it — and the minor may instead choose to affirm it. That is the practical difference from void, and the one students merge: voidable contracts operate until someone acts.

(c) Unenforceable under the Statute of Frauds — but not worthless. Unenforceable is not void, and part performance is exactly the doctrine these facts raise: possession, payment, and improvements in reliance. Whether it applies is a legal question. A licensee should know the doctrine exists so as not to tell a client an oral agreement is worthless, and should route it rather than answer it.

(d) The provision is unenforceable, and the rest of the lease may stand. The habitability obligation is not waivable, and the clause fails whether or not both parties agreed to it.

Problem 5

A seller in her late eighties seems confused during the listing appointment, asks the same questions repeatedly, and at one point does not recall that her husband died. Her son, who brought the licensee in, says she is "sharp as ever" and urges signing today. The licensee notes in the file that the seller "appeared to lack capacity."

What should the licensee do, and what is wrong with the file note?

Solution. Stop, escalate to the broker, and route it to counsel. Do not sign today, and do not proceed on the theory that she seemed fine or that a family member vouched for her.

A licensee's concern is authority, not diagnosis. A licensee is not qualified to assess mental capacity, and the file note characterizes her capacity — which is exactly the conclusion the licensee may not draw and which will be read later by people who were not there.

What the note should record instead is observation: what was said, what was asked repeatedly, what the son said and when, that the licensee did not proceed, and that the matter was escalated on a stated date. Observation, not inference — the same discipline as recording ceiling staining rather than diagnosing a roof leak.

Two further flags: the son's pressure to sign today is exactly the pattern that raises undue influence, and depending on the circumstances a contract with an incapacitated person may be voidable, or void where a conservatorship applies. All of that is for counsel.

Problem 6

The parties agree during escrow to move closing back one week. The agents confirm by email, escrow is told, and everyone proceeds. The seller also verbally agrees to leave the washer and dryer. The transaction fails and the parties dispute who breached.

What is the operative contract?

Solution. The original closing date, and no obligation about the appliances.

A change to a contract term is made by written amendment signed by both parties and delivered to escrow so the instructions match the agreement. An email between the agents does not amend the contract — the agents are not the parties. Neither does a verbal agreement between the parties, an instruction to escrow alone, or a shared understanding that a short extension "won't matter."

The parties are now litigating on a contract whose closing date is the original one, with an email chain between non-parties as the evidence of a change.

The appliances fail for the same reason plus one more: the agreement concerns an interest in real property within the Statute of Frauds, and personal property that does not convey unless included has not been included in any writing.

The practical rule: every agreement affecting the transaction goes in a signed writing. The boundary of what strictly must be written is not obvious in the moment, which is exactly why the practice is to write everything.

Problem 7

The buyer's investigation contingency period ends on the 17th. Nothing is delivered. On the 18th the seller's agent tells the seller the contingency expired, the buyer is committed, and she may accept a better offer that arrived overnight. Separately, the buyer waived the appraisal contingency to win the property, and the appraisal comes in $20,000 low.

Correct the first, and state what the licensee owed the buyer on the second.

Solution. All three statements about the contingency are wrong. Under the standard California form, contingencies remain in effect until the buyer removes them in writing — they are not self-executing on a date. The buyer has not removed anything, so his protection is intact, he is not committed, and the seller is not free to sell elsewhere. The seller's route is the contractual notice, which starts the period the contract specifies; if the buyer removes during it the transaction continues, and if not the seller may cancel by the contract's procedure.

The durable habit is better than the rule: read the contract's own removal mechanism. Different forms and negotiated terms operate differently.

On the waiver, what was owed before he decided: an explanation in writing of what the contingency protected and what waiving it exposed him to — that he could still investigate but would have no contractual path to act on what he found, and that a low appraisal would narrow him to bringing funds, renegotiating without leverage, or defaulting with his deposit exposed. Then follow his informed decision.

Both failure modes are wrong: refusing to write the offer overstates the licensee's role; writing it without comment abandons the advisory duty.

Problem 8

A buyer's loan is denied. He phones the listing agent, emails escrow demanding his deposit, and stops responding. The listing agent tells her seller the contract is over, that she may keep the deposit, and that the buyer "clearly materially breached." The buyer's agent tells him he will "definitely get it back" and should sue for specific performance if the seller resists.

Identify every error and state the correct posture.

Solution. Errors on both sides, and almost all of them are legal conclusions.

The buyer forfeited his protection rather than exercising it. A denial does not end the contract by itself; the loan contingency provides a path with requirements — the written notice the contract requires, within its terms, with supporting documentation. A phone call to the other agent is not that notice; a unilateral instruction to escrow is not cancellation, since escrow acts only on mutual written instructions; and ceasing to perform invites cancellation for non-performance, a materially worse position. Cancellation is a procedure, not an announcement.

The listing agent gave three wrong answers. Whether a breach is material is a legal question. Whether the seller may keep the deposit is a legal question — and any liquidated damages provision must have been properly agreed, is constrained by law, and generally limits recovery rather than adding to it. And the contract is not "over" because a date passed.

The buyer's agent gave two. "You'll definitely get it back" is a legal conclusion he is not entitled to give. And specific performance is a remedy for compelling performance — available for real property because of uniqueness, which is Lesson 01's physical characteristic producing a legal rule — not a route to recovering a deposit.

The correct posture, for both: explain the mechanism — the contract has a cancellation procedure with a written notice requirement, escrow acts only on mutual instructions, and a disputed deposit stays put until resolved. Get the notice right, document everything with dates, escalate to the broker, and get the client an answer from counsel before the deadline runs.

Chapter summary

Four elements form a contract: mutual assent, consideration, capacity, lawful object.

Classify on four axes — express or implied, bilateral or unilateral, executory or executed, and by enforceability. "Executed" in classification means performed, not signed.

Three formation rules resolve most questions: an offer accepted without change forms a contract; an acceptance must match the offer; acceptance must be communicated.

A counteroffer rejects and replaces. The original is gone, not suspended — and a signature with a change written on it is a further counteroffer.

An offer can be revoked before acceptance even where it states a deadline, unless consideration made it an option.

Adequacy of consideration is generally not examined; past consideration generally is not consideration.

Capacity is a matter for authority and referral, never diagnosis. Record observations, not characterizations, and escalate.

Void, voidable, and unenforceable are three different outcomes. A voidable contract is binding until the entitled party elects to avoid it — and may be affirmed instead.

The Statute of Frauds requires a signed writing for sales of real property, leases over a year, and compensation agreements. Non-compliance makes an agreement unenforceable, not void, and part performance may still reach it.

Only a signed written amendment changes a contract term. Agent emails, verbal agreements, and escrow instructions alone change nothing.

A contingency conditions an obligation inside a formed contract, and under the standard California form it ends only by written removal — never by a passed date.

Read the contract's definitions of how time is counted. Being wrong by one day costs a client a right.

Distinguish assignment from novation, and explain a waiver's real exposure in writing before the client decides.

Specific performance is available for real property because land is unique — the clearest case in the course of a legal rule flowing from a physical characteristic.

Liquidated damages must be properly agreed, are constrained by law, and generally limit recovery.

Cancellation is a procedure; rescission is a remedy. They are not synonyms.

Never tell a client whether they may cancel, whether a breach is material, or who gets the deposit. Explain the mechanism, follow the contract's procedures, document, escalate, and refer before the deadline.

Required applied assignment

Prepare a one-page file memorandum for the applied scenario presented with this assignment. Trace the formation sequence and state whether a contract exists and on whose terms, identify any element or assent defect and classify the result as void, voidable, or unenforceable, state which agreements in the scenario must be in a signed writing and what actually amends the contract, identify each contingency in effect and what would be required to remove it, state the notice the next step requires and its delivery method, identify every question you would decline to answer and why, and state what you would escalate to the broker and refer to counsel and by what deadline. The instructor version contains the scoring rubric.

Knowledge check and remediation

Complete the five-item lesson quiz in the secure learning platform. The lesson mastery threshold is 80 percent — four of the five items. An unsuccessful attempt opens targeted remediation: an alternate explanation of the concepts, a second worked scenario, and a different five-item set covering the same concepts. The 80 percent threshold is a StateCourse instructional policy proposed for DRE review; it is not represented as a DRE-mandated score.

Assignment completion

Completion requires all six instructional segments, the applied memorandum, the quiz submission, and any triggered remediation. Assignment completion does not waive the separate final examination, minimum elapsed-time, identity, proctor, or approval requirements.

Assessment materials for this assignment

These are the assessment items the student is served inside this assignment. In the course itself the student sees only the question and the answer choices — the correct answer and the explanation are withheld until the item has been answered, and the explanation for a failed engagement check is withheld while the student works the remediation set. They are printed here in full because this volume is submitted for review, and a reviewer is entitled to the item, the key and the reasoning.

Applied exercise — 100% required to complete the assignment

1. A seller and buyer shake hands on a price for a home and exchange text messages confirming the number and the closing month. The buyer then spends money on an inspection. The seller receives a higher offer and refuses to proceed, saying nothing was ever signed. The buyer asks the licensee whether he has a contract. What should the licensee say?

  1. A. Explain that contracts for the sale of real property generally must be in writing to be enforceable, that whether these communications satisfy that requirement is a legal question, and refer the buyer to an attorney rather than giving him an answer.
  2. B. Tell the buyer he has an enforceable contract, since the text messages record the essential terms and he relied on them.
  3. C. Tell the buyer he has no contract of any kind, since a handshake and texts cannot create obligations for real property.
  4. D. Tell the buyer that his inspection expense makes the agreement enforceable regardless of the writing requirement.

Answer: A. The writing requirement for real property contracts is the governing principle, but whether particular electronic communications satisfy it, and whether the buyer's reliance changes the analysis, are legal questions with real complexity. Answering either way would be practicing law on a question the licensee cannot resolve.

Engagement check — 5 items, 80% required

1. Which elements are required to form a valid contract?

  1. A. Capable parties, mutual consent, a lawful object, and consideration.
  2. B. A written document, signatures, notarization, and recording.
  3. C. An offer, an acceptance, a deposit, and a closing date.
  4. D. Mutual consent, a lawful object, and a licensed intermediary.

Answer: A. Capacity, mutual consent, lawful object, and consideration are the essential elements. Notarization, recording, deposits, and intermediaries are transaction features rather than formation requirements.

2. What is the effect of a counteroffer on the original offer?

  1. A. It rejects the original offer and substitutes a new one, so the original can no longer be accepted unless it is renewed.
  2. B. It suspends the original offer, which may be accepted if the counteroffer is rejected.
  3. C. It modifies the original offer while leaving it otherwise in force.
  4. D. It has no legal effect until the original offeror responds to it.

Answer: A. A counteroffer terminates the original offer's power of acceptance. It neither suspends nor amends the original, and it takes effect as a new offer on communication.

3. What does the Statute of Frauds require in a real estate context?

  1. A. That contracts for the sale of real property, and certain other agreements, be in writing and signed to be enforceable.
  2. B. That all real estate contracts be notarized before they take effect.
  3. C. That real estate contracts be recorded to bind the parties.
  4. D. That real estate contracts be prepared by an attorney.

Answer: A. The requirement is a signed writing for enforceability. Notarization, recording, and attorney preparation are not what the doctrine requires.

4. A minor signs a purchase agreement for real property. What is the likely status of the contract?

  1. A. It is generally voidable, because capacity is an element of a valid contract and a minor's contracts may typically be disaffirmed.
  2. B. It is void from the outset and has no effect whatsoever.
  3. C. It is fully valid and enforceable against the minor.
  4. D. It is valid if a parent was present when it was signed.

Answer: A. Capacity problems generally make a contract voidable at the incapacitated party's election rather than void. A parent's presence does not supply the minor's capacity.

5. What remedy does specific performance provide?

  1. A. A court order requiring a party to perform the contract, available where damages would be inadequate — as is often argued for real property because each parcel is unique.
  2. B. Money damages calculated to compensate the non-breaching party's losses.
  3. C. Cancellation of the contract and restoration of the parties to their prior positions.
  4. D. An amount fixed in advance by the parties as compensation for breach.

Answer: A. Specific performance compels performance itself. The other three describe damages, rescission, and liquidated damages respectively.

Remediation set — served only after a failed engagement check

1. An offer states it will remain open until Friday. The offeror withdraws it on Wednesday, before acceptance. What is the general rule?

  1. A. An offer may generally be revoked before acceptance unless it is supported by consideration as an option, so the stated deadline does not by itself bind the offeror.
  2. B. The offer must remain open until Friday because the offeror stated a deadline.
  3. C. The offer may be revoked only if the offeree has not yet begun to consider it.
  4. D. The offer becomes irrevocable as soon as the offeree receives it.

Answer: A. A stated deadline sets an outer limit but does not create irrevocability; consideration is what turns an offer into a binding option. Receipt and the offeree's deliberation do not bind the offeror.

2. What distinguishes rescission from a claim for damages?

  1. A. Rescission unwinds the contract and seeks to restore the parties to their prior positions, while damages leave the contract's effect intact and compensate for the loss.
  2. B. Rescission is available only for fraud, while damages are available for any breach.
  3. C. Rescission is granted by the parties, while damages are granted by a court.
  4. D. Rescission applies to real property contracts and damages apply to personal property contracts.

Answer: A. The two remedies point in opposite directions: undoing the bargain versus compensating within it. Rescission is not limited to fraud and not limited by property type, and both can be pursued through the courts.

3. A contract's performance is conditioned on the buyer obtaining financing. What kind of provision is this?

  1. A. A condition, which qualifies the duty to perform without preventing the contract from being formed.
  2. B. A covenant, which is a promise that the buyer will obtain financing.
  3. C. A warranty, which guarantees the financing will be obtained.
  4. D. An option, which gives the buyer the right to decide whether to proceed.

Answer: A. A condition qualifies performance within a formed contract. A covenant would promise the outcome, a warranty would guarantee it, and an option would give an unconditional election.

4. Parties agree in advance that a specified deposit will be the seller's sole recovery if the buyer defaults. What is this called?

  1. A. A liquidated damages provision, which fixes the recovery in advance and is subject to legal limits on enforceability.
  2. B. A penalty clause, which is enforceable as written between sophisticated parties.
  3. C. An option payment, which compensates the seller for holding the property.
  4. D. A forfeiture provision, which is automatically enforceable in real property contracts.

Answer: A. Fixing damages in advance is liquidated damages, and its enforceability is constrained by law — which is exactly why a provision that operates as a penalty is treated differently. It is not an option payment and it is not automatically enforceable.

5. A contract's stated purpose is an activity that is illegal. What is the effect?

  1. A. The contract fails for want of a lawful object and is generally void, since legality is an element of formation.
  2. B. The contract is voidable at the election of the party who did not know of the illegality.
  3. C. The contract is enforceable if both parties knew of the illegality when they signed.
  4. D. The contract is enforceable except as to the illegal portion, which is simply ignored.

Answer: A. Lawful object is a formation element, so its absence is more serious than a defect making a contract voidable. Mutual knowledge does not cure it, and severing an illegal core purpose is not available.

Real Estate Principles - Lesson Assignment 09

Transfer, deeds, title, and recording

Course version: 1.0 submission draft Assignment time: 180 instructional minutes Regulatory status: Not approved; no California credit is available.

Learning objectives

  • State the requirements of a valid deed and identify which common assumptions about deeds are wrong.
  • Distinguish a grant deed from a quitclaim deed and other deed types by what each warrants.
  • Explain delivery and acceptance and why a signed, recorded deed can still fail to transfer title.
  • Explain recording, the notice it gives, and how priority is determined.
  • Describe title insurance and read a preliminary report as an allocation of risk.
  • Distinguish voluntary from involuntary transfer and identify what each requires.

Timed sequence

ActivityMinutesEvidence
Guided reading: deed requirements and deed types55Sections 1-2 viewed and notes saved
Guided reading: delivery, acceptance, and recording50Sections 3-4 viewed
Guided reading: title insurance and involuntary transfer45Sections 5-6 viewed
Applied scenario and decision memorandum20Written response submitted
Lesson assessment10Five scored items submitted
Total180One of 15 separate lesson assignments

1. Deed requirements

1.1 What a deed is

A deed is the written instrument by which an owner conveys an interest in real property to another. The parties have specific names:

  • Grantor — the party conveying.
  • Grantee — the party receiving.

A memory device that survives the examination: the grantor gives; the grantee takes.

1.2 The requirements

A valid deed must generally:

RequirementDetail
Be in writingThe Statute of Frauds applies to conveyances
Identify a competent grantorLegally capable, and with authority to convey
Identify the granteeSufficiently to be ascertainable
Describe the propertyAdequately — not by street address alone
Contain granting languageWords showing present intent to convey
Be signed by the grantorThe grantee's signature is generally not required
Be delivered and acceptedSection 3 — and the requirement most often misunderstood

1.3 What a deed does not require

Students and clients believe several things a deed does not need, and each misbelief causes real problems.

Consideration is not required for validity. A deed may be a gift. Consideration matters for other purposes — including whether a party qualifies as a bona fide purchaser under the recording system — but a deed reciting "love and affection" can be perfectly valid.

The grantee need not sign. The grantor conveys; the grantee's acceptance is required but is generally presumed where the conveyance is beneficial.

Recording is not required for validity. A deed transfers title between grantor and grantee on delivery and acceptance, recorded or not. Recording protects against third parties — it does not create the transfer.

Notarization is not required for validity, but it is required in practice: a deed must generally be acknowledged before a notary to be recorded. So an unacknowledged deed may be valid and unrecordable, which is a problem the grantee will discover later.

A perfect legal description is not required if the property is otherwise adequately described, but adequacy is a legal question and the practice is to use the recorded legal description exactly.

1.4 The granting clause

The words showing intent to convey — "grant," "convey," "quitclaim." In California the word "grant" carries statutory significance, discussed in Section 2, which is why deed type follows from the operative word rather than from the document's title.

1.5 The habendum and other clauses

The habendum clause — historically "to have and to hold" — defines the extent of the estate conveyed. Where it conflicts with the granting clause, the resolution is a legal question.

Reservations and exceptions carve something out: a reserved life estate, reserved mineral rights, an excepted strip. These are the "except" and "reserving" phrases from Lesson 04, and dropping one while copying describes a different parcel.

Conditions and restrictions may appear, and conditional language in a deed is a title matter for counsel, not a curiosity.

1.6 The licensee's practice

  1. Take the legal description from a recorded document, not from a prior listing.
  2. Copy it exactly and completely, including recording references and every reservation, exception, and "together with."
  3. Never substitute an address or APN.
  4. Escrow prepares the deed; the licensee confirms the vesting instruction came from the client after the client consulted counsel.
  5. Route conditional or unusual language to title and to counsel.

1.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to list the requirements of a valid deed and name four things a deed does not require.

2. Grant deed and quitclaim deed

2.1 The spectrum

Deeds differ in what the grantor warrants about the title being conveyed. That is the organizing idea; the names follow from it.

DeedWhat the grantor warrants
General warranty deedThe broadest warranties, extending back through prior ownership. Uncommon in California residential practice
Grant deedLimited implied warranties (Section 2.2). The standard California residential instrument
Quitclaim deedNothing. Conveys whatever interest the grantor has, which may be none
Trustee's deedGiven following a trustee's sale under a deed of trust
Sheriff's deedGiven following an execution sale
Gift deedA conveyance for love and affection rather than value
Deed in lieu of foreclosureA borrower conveying to the lender to avoid foreclosure

2.2 The grant deed's implied warranties

By use of the word "grant," a California grantor impliedly warrants two things unless the deed says otherwise:

  1. That the grantor has not previously conveyed the same estate to another.
  2. That the estate is free from encumbrances made or suffered by the grantor — not by prior owners.

Both warranties are limited to the grantor's own period of ownership. A grant deed does not warrant against a defect created by someone who owned the property in 1974.

That limit is exactly why title insurance exists in California residential practice: the deed's warranties do not reach the risks the buyer actually faces.

2.3 The quitclaim deed

A quitclaim conveys whatever interest the grantor has, with no warranty that the grantor has any.

Its legitimate uses are specific and common:

  • Clearing a cloud on title — a possible claimant releases whatever interest they might have.
  • Transfers between related parties where warranties are unnecessary.
  • Correcting a defect in a prior conveyance.
  • Releasing an easement or other interest.

What a quitclaim does not do: it does not clear liens against the property, and it does not make the grantee's title better than the grantor's was. A buyer receiving a quitclaim in an arm's-length purchase should understand that if the grantor owned nothing, the buyer received nothing.

A licensee must not advise a client to accept a quitclaim, or to give one, as a solution to a title problem. Whether a quitclaim resolves a particular cloud is a legal question, and quitclaims are also used to accomplish frauds precisely because they warrant nothing.

2.4 Deed types encountered after default

A trustee's deed conveys title following a trustee's sale. A buyer at such a sale takes what the sale conveys — which may extinguish junior liens but not senior ones — and the property is generally sold without the protections of an ordinary transaction.

A deed in lieu of foreclosure transfers title to the lender voluntarily. It does not automatically extinguish junior liens, which is the reason a lender may decline one, and its consequences for the borrower are legal and tax questions.

Both belong to Lesson 11's default material. Here the point is recognition: a chain of title containing one of these tells a story the buyer's counsel and title company should read.

2.5 Reconveyance

Not a transfer of ownership but of a security interest: the reconveyance is the recorded document releasing a deed of trust when the debt is satisfied.

Payment of the debt does not clear the record; the recorded document does. A seller who says a loan was paid off years ago has stated a fact about the debt and nothing about the title, and an unreleased deed of trust in a preliminary report requires a document.

2.6 Checkpoint

You should be able to state what a grant deed impliedly warrants and its limit, and explain what a quitclaim does and does not accomplish.

3. Delivery and acceptance

3.1 The requirement that surprises everyone

A deed transfers title on delivery and acceptance. Signing does not transfer title. Notarizing does not transfer title. Recording does not transfer title.

A deed that is signed, notarized, and sitting in a drawer has conveyed nothing.

3.2 What delivery means

Delivery is not primarily physical. It is the grantor's present intent to pass title now, manifested by conduct.

The recurring evidence of intent:

EvidenceWeight
Handing the deed to the granteeStrong
Recording the deedRaises a presumption of delivery
Delivering to escrow with instructions to record on closingDelivery on the conditions being met
Handing it to a third party for the granteeDepends on the instructions and the grantor's control
Keeping it, with instructions to record after deathGenerally not effective delivery — the grantor retained control and intended a testamentary transfer

The failure mode is intent, not custody. A grantor who hands over a deed while saying "this takes effect when I die" has not manifested present intent to pass title now, and the attempted transfer generally fails as an ineffective testamentary act.

3.3 Delivery to escrow

Escrow supplies the ordinary mechanism. The grantor deposits the deed with instructions to deliver on the conditions being satisfied. That is a conditional delivery, and it is one of the two elements — with a binding contract — that make an arrangement an escrow at all.

Critically, once delivered into escrow under a binding contract, the grantor generally cannot unilaterally recall it. The escrow holder is not the grantor's agent for that purpose.

3.4 Acceptance

The grantee must accept. Acceptance is generally presumed where the conveyance is beneficial, and it can be shown by conduct — recording, taking possession, paying taxes, encumbering the property.

Acceptance matters most where it is refused. A grantee can decline a conveyance, and there are real reasons to: contaminated property carrying remediation liability, property carrying assessments exceeding its value, or an unwanted interest in a dispute.

3.5 What a void delivery cannot be cured by

Recording does not cure a defective delivery. A recorded deed raises a presumption of delivery, and a presumption can be rebutted. A deed recorded by a grantee who took it from a drawer without the grantor's intent to convey did not become effective by being recorded.

This is also the mechanism behind deed fraud: a forged or improperly delivered deed appears in the record and looks like a conveyance. A forged deed is void and conveys nothing, no matter how many transfers follow it — which is why the title industry treats forgery as a category of loss distinct from an ordinary defect.

3.6 The licensee's role

Delivery and acceptance questions arise in specific situations a licensee should be able to spot:

  • A client says a relative "signed the house over" years ago but nothing was recorded and nothing changed.
  • A deed appears in the record that the seller says he never signed.
  • A parent wants to deed the property to a child "but keep it until I die."
  • A grantee wants to refuse a conveyance.

In every one, the licensee's role is the same: recognize, stop, escalate to the broker, and route it to title and to counsel. Whether a delivery was effective is a legal conclusion with enormous consequences.

3.7 Checkpoint

You should be able to explain why a signed and notarized deed may convey nothing, and identify a delivery that fails for lack of present intent.

4. Recording and constructive notice

4.1 What the recording system is for

California maintains a public record of documents affecting real property. The system exists to answer one question:

Who has notice of what?

Recording does not make a document valid, and failing to record does not make it invalid between the parties. Recording protects the recorded party against third parties.

4.2 The three kinds of notice

TypeWhat it is
Actual noticeThe person in fact knows
Constructive noticeThe law charges the person with knowing, because it was recorded
Inquiry noticeFacts that would prompt a reasonable person to investigate

Constructive notice is the system's engine. A recorded document is knowable by anyone who looks, so the law treats everyone as knowing it. That is why a buyer cannot claim to be surprised by a recorded easement he never read.

Inquiry notice is the one that surprises people, because nothing was recorded. Someone visibly in possession who is not the record owner, a well-worn path across the rear of a lot, an occupant paying rent to a person other than the seller — each is a fact that would prompt investigation, and a purchaser may be charged with what the investigation would have revealed.

4.3 The bona fide purchaser

The recording system's protection generally runs to a bona fide purchaser: one who takes for value, in good faith, and without notice of the prior interest — actual, constructive, or inquiry.

Each element does work:

  • For value is why a donee is treated differently from a buyer, and one reason consideration matters even though a deed does not require it for validity.
  • In good faith excludes a party who knew of the problem.
  • Without notice includes what the records showed and what an inquiry would have revealed.

4.4 Priority

The general rule: first in time, first in right, as measured by recording, for those entitled to the system's protection.

The exceptions from Lesson 05, restated because they belong to the recording material:

ExceptionEffect
Property tax liensGenerally take priority regardless of when they attached
Mechanic's liensPriority may relate back to when work commenced
Subordination agreementA lienholder agrees to take a lower position
Purchase-money priorityCertain purchase-money security interests receive favored treatment

Priority determines who is paid first from a limited fund and whose interest survives a foreclosure. A junior lienholder wiped out by a senior foreclosure has lost its security whatever the merits of the debt — which is why a recording date on a preliminary report is not administrative detail.

4.5 The chain of title and the abstract

The chain of title is the successive recorded conveyances tracing ownership. A break in the chain — a conveyance from someone who never appears as a grantee — is a defect requiring resolution.

A wild deed is a recorded document outside the chain: because a searcher following the chain would not find it, recording it may not give constructive notice.

An abstract of title is a summary of the recorded documents affecting a parcel. In modern California residential practice the preliminary report and the title policy have largely replaced reliance on an abstract, but the vocabulary persists.

4.6 What is recorded and what is not

Recorded: deeds, deeds of trust, reconveyances, easements, declarations of restrictions, judgment abstracts, mechanic's liens, lis pendens, maps, and many other instruments.

Frequently not recorded, and therefore invisible to a records search: leases, occupancy agreements, unrecorded easements arising by implication or prescription, side agreements between parties, and personal property arrangements.

That gap is what inquiry notice covers, and it is why physical inspection of the property is a separate obligation from reading the title report.

4.8 The recording statute, and what "void as against" means

Section 4.1 said that recording gives constructive notice and protects a purchaser. Civil Code § 1214 is the section that does it, and its wording repays close reading because it is a race-notice rule expressed as a rule of voidness:

"Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein, other than a lease for a term not exceeding one year, is void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee of the same property, or any part thereof, in good faith and for a valuable consideration, whose conveyance is first duly recorded, and as against any judgment affecting the title, unless the conveyance shall have been duly recorded prior to the record of notice of action."

Unpack it as four conditions a later buyer must satisfy to defeat an earlier unrecorded conveyance.

ConditionThe wordsWhat it excludes
Subsequent"any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee"Someone who took first cannot use the section
In good faith"in good faith"A buyer with actual notice of the earlier deed
For value"for a valuable consideration"A donee; an heir; a gift
First recorded"whose conveyance is first duly recorded"A later buyer who also failed to record

All four, together. This is California's race-notice system in a sentence: the later purchaser must be both without notice and first to record. Neither alone is enough.

"Void as against" is narrower than "void." The unrecorded deed is perfectly good between the grantor and the grantee. It fails only against a person the section describes. A grantee who never records still owns the property against the whole world except a subsequent good-faith purchaser for value who records first — which is exactly the person most likely to appear.

The lease carve-out is a practical one. A lease for a term not exceeding one year is outside the section. Short residential tenancies are not recorded and were never expected to be, and a buyer of occupied property takes subject to what possession discloses regardless.

And the tail reaches judgments: "and as against any judgment affecting the title, unless the conveyance shall have been duly recorded prior to the record of notice of action." An unrecorded deed can lose to a judgment in litigation the grantee knew nothing about.

4.9 Why possession still matters after recording

§ 1214 protects a purchaser "in good faith." Good faith is defeated by notice, and notice is not only what the records show.

Constructive notice comes from two places. The recorded chain of title, and the fact of possession. A person in open, visible, exclusive possession of property puts a prospective purchaser on inquiry: the purchaser is charged with knowing what a reasonable inquiry of that occupant would have revealed.

This is why a walk-through is a title procedure and not only a condition procedure. An occupant who is not the seller is a question. A tenant with a five-year unrecorded lease, a relative with an unrecorded life estate, a buyer under an unrecorded contract of sale — none appears in the records and each appears at the property.

The practical instruction for a licensee is one sentence long: if anyone other than the seller is in possession, find out in writing who they are and on what basis, and give the answer to escrow and to the title company before closing.

4.10 A worked priority problem

1 March. Owner deeds the property to Buyer A for $700,000. A takes the deed home and does not record it. 14 March. Owner deeds the same property to Buyer B for $720,000. B has never heard of A, searches title and finds nothing, and records on 15 March. 20 March. A records.

B prevails. B is a subsequent purchaser, in good faith (no actual or constructive notice — nothing was recorded and, on these facts, nobody was in possession), for valuable consideration, whose conveyance was first duly recorded. A's earlier deed is "void as against" B under § 1214.

Change one fact. Suppose A had moved in on 2 March and was living there when B inspected.

Now B loses, and not because of the recording dates. A's open possession is inquiry notice; B is charged with what an inquiry of the occupant would have revealed, which is A's deed. B is no longer a purchaser "in good faith," and the first condition of § 1214 fails. The recording race is irrelevant because B cannot get past the good-faith requirement.

Change a different fact. Suppose the 14 March transfer was a gift to Owner's nephew, who recorded immediately.

A prevails. The nephew is subsequent and first to record and may well be in good faith, but he did not take "for a valuable consideration." § 1214 does not protect him.

The lesson a licensee should carry from all three: recording is decisive only when the other three conditions are met, and the two that fail most often in real life are good faith, defeated by someone living in the house, and value, defeated by a family transfer. Both are visible before closing to anyone who looks.

4.11 The disclosure article, and the waiver that is void

One more section belongs in a chapter about what passes with the transfer. Civil Code § 1102 opens the residential transfer disclosure article:

"(a) Except as provided in Section 1102.2, this article applies to any transfer by sale, exchange, real property sales contract as defined in Section 2985, lease with an option to purchase, any other option to purchase, or ground lease coupled with improvements of any single-family residential property.

(b) For purposes of this article, the definitions contained in Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 10000) of Part 1 of Division 4 of the Business and Professions Code shall apply.

(c) Any waiver of the requirements of this article is void as against public policy."

Subdivision (a) is broader than "sale." A lease with an option, a bare option, and a ground lease coupled with improvements are all inside the article. A transaction structured to avoid a sale does not thereby avoid the disclosure obligation.

Subdivision (b) is the cross-reference from Assignment 01 Section 5.8 — the Civil Code borrowing the Business and Professions Code's definitions. A reader of the disclosure article who does not know that is reading with a piece missing.

Subdivision (c) is one short sentence and it settles a great deal. "Any waiver of the requirements of this article is void as against public policy." A seller cannot contract out of it. A buyer cannot agree to give it up, however sophisticated they are and however much they are paid for the concession. A licensee presented with an "as-is, no disclosures" arrangement should know that the words do not do what the parties think they do.

4.12 Checkpoint

You should be able to explain what recording does and does not accomplish, define the three kinds of notice, and state the elements of a bona fide purchaser.

5. Title insurance and preliminary reports

5.1 What a preliminary report is

A preliminary report reports the condition of title as shown in the records and states the terms on which the title insurer would be willing to issue a policy, including the exceptions it would take.

Three things it is not:

  • Not a guarantee that title is clear.
  • Not the policy. It states terms; the policy is the contract.
  • Not a survey. It addresses record title, not the physical property.

5.2 Exceptions, exclusions, requirements

Three categories a licensee must distinguish:

CategoryWhat it is
ExceptionAn item the policy will not insure against. The buyer bears that risk unless it is otherwise addressed
ExclusionA category the policy form does not cover at all — governmental regulation such as zoning, eminent domain, matters created or agreed to by the insured
RequirementSomething the insurer needs before issuing — a reconveyance, a resolution, a release, evidence of authority

The requirements are the items with deadlines attached, and the ones most likely to delay a closing.

5.3 What the policy does

Title insurance indemnifies the insured against covered losses from title defects, within the policy's terms and excluding what it excepts. It also typically obligates the insurer to defend covered claims.

Two features distinguish it from other insurance:

It looks backward, not forward. Other insurance covers future events; title insurance covers defects that already exist in the record or the chain, discovered later.

The premium is generally paid once, at closing, for coverage that continues.

5.4 Owner's and lender's policies

The owner's policy insures the buyer's interest. The lender's policy insures the lender's lien and its priority.

They insure different interests, which is why both commonly exist — and why a buyer who declines an owner's policy because "there's a title policy on the loan" has not economized on a duplicate. He has left his own interest uninsured.

Extended coverage may address matters a standard policy excepts, including some survey matters, typically requiring a survey or other evidence. Whether to obtain it is the buyer's decision, made informed.

5.5 What title insurance does not cover

The list is as important as the coverage:

  • Zoning and governmental regulation — excluded.
  • Physical condition of the property.
  • Boundary location, under a standard policy — the survey exception.
  • Matters the insured created or agreed to.
  • Matters known to the insured and not disclosed to the insurer.
  • Anything the policy excepted.

A buyer asks whether the neighbor's fence is on the line and the agent says the title report "came back clean."

That answer is wrong. The report addresses record title, and boundary location is exactly what the standard policy excepts. Nothing in the report speaks to where the fence is. A survey does.

5.6 Reading the report item by item

ItemCorrect handling
Utility easement along a boundaryObtain the document — width, location, permitted use. Can prevent structures the buyer intends
Recorded CC&RsObtain and review; bind the buyer regardless of zoning
Unreleased deed of trust the seller says was paidA recorded reconveyance must be obtained
Mechanic's lienRoute to escrow and title; priority may relate back
Judgment against a similarly named personRoute to title; do not assume it is or is not the seller
Lis pendensA serious cloud; route to counsel
A requirement for a corporate resolution or trustee evidenceThe authority verification from Lesson 03, with a deadline

Three responses wrong in every case: treating an item as routine because most properties have one; asking title to "remove" an exception; and predicting an easement's or restriction's effect on the buyer's plans.

5.7 The timing point

The preliminary report and the underlying documents belong at the front of the transaction queue, with association documents and hazard-area insurance quotes.

An exception discovered late — an easement across the building site, an unreleased lien requiring a document from a lender that no longer exists — takes time to resolve. A buyer who receives the report on day three has options; one who receives it on day twelve of a fourteen-day review has a formality.

5.9 What the two policies cover, side by side

Section 5.4 named owner's and lender's policies. The difference is not a matter of degree, and a buyer who declines an owner's policy on the ground that "the lender has one" has misunderstood what they were declining.

Owner's policyLender's policy
InsuredThe buyerThe lender
AmountThe purchase priceThe loan amount
DurationAs long as the insured holds an interest, and beyond for warranties of titleUntil the loan is paid
Behaviour over timeStays at the purchase priceDeclines as the loan amortises
On a claimPays the ownerPays the lender; the owner recovers nothing

The lender's policy does not protect the buyer at all. If a title defect surfaces and there is no owner's policy, the lender is made whole and the buyer bears the entire loss of their equity — the down payment, every principal payment made, and the property.

And an owner's policy is the cheapest insurance in the transaction on a per-dollar basis, because it is issued once for a single premium and never renewed.

5.10 Reading Schedule B, and the four exception types

A preliminary report is not a policy. It is an offer to issue a policy on stated terms, and the terms are the exceptions in Schedule B. Four types appear, and they call for different responses.

Monetary liens. Deeds of trust, judgments, tax liens, mechanics liens. These are cleared at closing — paid from proceeds and released. Their presence is a payoff question, not a title question.

Easements and rights of way. Utility easements, access easements, drainage. These do not clear. They travel with the land, and the question is whether they affect the buyer's intended use. A utility easement across the back of a lot is ordinary; the same easement across the only buildable area is a different property from the one the buyer thinks they are buying.

Covenants, conditions and restrictions. Recorded restrictions on use, and in a common interest development the declaration. These do not clear either, and they are frequently the most consequential document in the file.

Survey and boundary exceptions. "Any facts an accurate survey would disclose." This exception is the title company declining to insure the boundaries, and it is standard on the basic policy. A buyer who wants the boundaries insured is buying extended coverage and, usually, providing a survey.

The habit that catches problems: read Schedule B against the buyer's stated plans. A buyer who intends to build a workshop, park a boat, run a home business, add a second unit, or fence the perimeter is a buyer for whom a specific exception may matter, and the licensee is the only person who knows both the plan and the report.

5.11 A worked exception

A buyer intends to build a detached garage on the north side of the lot. Schedule B, item 7: "An easement for ingress, egress and public utilities over the northerly 12 feet of said land, as granted to Southern California Edison Company by instrument recorded [date], in Book [x], Page [y] of Official Records."

Nothing about this clears at closing, and no amount of money paid at escrow makes it go away.

Three actions, in order. Obtain the recorded instrument itself — the report gives its book and page, and the report's one-line description is a summary, not the grant. Compare its width and location against a plot plan or survey. Then determine whether the intended garage sits inside the twelve feet.

If it does, the buyer's plan is not feasible as conceived, and the options — relocating the structure, seeking a quitclaim or partial release from the utility, or withdrawing — are questions for the utility, the city and counsel respectively.

The licensee's whole job here is timing. Every step above is available in the first week of escrow and impossible in the last. The failure mode is not missing the exception; it is reading it, understanding it, and forwarding it without connecting it to what the buyer said they wanted to do.

5.12 Checkpoint

You should be able to explain what an exception means, distinguish it from an exclusion and a requirement, and state what title insurance does not cover.

6. Voluntary and involuntary transfer

6.1 The two categories

Voluntary transfer occurs with the owner's intent: sale, gift, dedication, and transfer at death by will.

Involuntary transfer occurs without it: intestate succession, escheat, eminent domain, foreclosure, execution sale, tax sale, adverse possession, and transfers by operation of natural forces.

6.2 Transfer at death

Testate — the decedent left a valid will. Real property passes as the will directs, generally through probate unless a mechanism avoids it.

Intestate — no valid will. Property passes by intestate succession to heirs in the order the law specifies. That order is statutory and its application is legal work.

Escheat — no will and no heirs who take. The property passes to the state.

Probate is the court-supervised process of administering a decedent's estate. Sales during probate may require court involvement and may follow particular procedures — which is why the personal representative's authority must be verified against the appointment, exactly as Lesson 03 required.

Mechanisms that can avoid probate — a trust holding title, survivorship forms of ownership, and certain statutory instruments — have different consequences and are estate planning matters for counsel.

6.3 Adverse possession

Title acquired through possession meeting statutory requirements. The elements are conventionally described as possession that is open and notorious, hostile to the true owner's interest, actual, exclusive, and continuous for the statutory period — and in California, payment of taxes is also required.

Two points for a licensee:

The tax payment requirement is the practical filter. It defeats most casual claims, because a person occupying without paying the taxes generally cannot satisfy it.

It is a legal doctrine, never a licensee's conclusion. A client who says "we've used that strip for twenty years, so it's ours" has stated a claim requiring legal analysis — and the neighbor who says "they've used it so long there's nothing I can do" has stated the mirror image. Both go to counsel.

Prescriptive easements arise from the same family of doctrines and produce a use right rather than ownership.

6.4 Transfer by natural forces

Accretion — the gradual addition of land by deposit — generally benefits the owner. Erosion is its gradual counterpart. Avulsion — a sudden change, such as a river changing course in a storm — generally does not shift boundaries. Reliction is land exposed by a permanent recession of water.

These matter on waterfront and watercourse property and are boundary questions for a surveyor and counsel.

6.5 Involuntary transfer after default

Foreclosure — judicial or nonjudicial — transfers title following default under a security instrument, and is the subject of Lesson 11.

Execution sale follows a judgment, transferring title by sheriff's deed.

Tax sale follows unpaid property taxes under the applicable process.

Each produces a deed type carrying its own limitations, and each appears in a chain of title as a signal that the buyer's counsel and title company should look closely.

6.6 Dedication

Dedication is a private owner devoting land to public use, accepted by the public body. It appears most often on subdivision maps, where streets and easements are offered for dedication as a condition of approval.

A licensee reading a recorded map should recognize dedicated areas as land the owner no longer controls — which occasionally surprises a buyer who measured the lot to the pavement.

6.7 What ties this lesson together

Every mechanism in this lesson answers one of three questions, and a licensee who keeps them separate will handle unfamiliar situations correctly:

  1. Did title actually transfer? — the deed requirements, and delivery and acceptance.
  2. Who has notice, and whose interest prevails? — recording and priority.
  3. What risk is insured, and what is not? — the policy, its exceptions, and its exclusions.

A licensee who can place a problem into one of those three, and route it accordingly, is doing the job. A licensee who answers it is not.

6.8 A worked title problem

A licensee takes a listing. The preliminary report reveals:

  • Title vested in a person who died two years ago.
  • A deed from that person to the current occupant, signed and notarized but never recorded.
  • A deed of trust recorded eighteen months ago, signed by the occupant.
  • A lien recorded against the deceased owner's name eleven months ago.

The occupant says: "My uncle gave me the house before he died. I have the deed."

What each element means, applying this lesson.

An unrecorded deed can still be effective between the parties. Section 3 establishes that delivery and acceptance are what transfer title, not recording. The occupant may well own the property.

Recording is about notice to the world. Section 4. An unrecorded deed does not give constructive notice, which means subsequent parties dealing with the record owner may take without knowledge of it — and the consequences depend on rules this course states and does not resolve on particular facts.

The eleven-month-old lien is the problem the unrecorded deed created. It was recorded against a person the record still showed as the owner, after the deed was signed and before it was recorded. Whether it attaches is exactly the question the recording system exists to answer, and it is a legal question with real stakes.

The deed of trust signed by the occupant was presumably underwritten on some showing of ownership, which raises its own questions about what the lender was given.

The delivery question is live. Section 3.2's requirements — was the deed delivered during the uncle's lifetime, with intent to pass title presently? "He gave it to me" describes a belief. A deed found in a drawer after death is a different fact pattern from a deed handed over with intent, and the difference determines whether title passed at all or whether the property is part of the estate.

What the licensee does.

He does not take the listing on the occupant's description. Lesson 03's intake questions apply with force: how is title held, may I see the document, who must sign.

He routes it — to counsel and to the title company — before marketing. Every one of the questions above is legal, and the title company will not insure until they are resolved.

He records what he was told and when, and he does not repeat the occupant's characterization of ownership in any advertisement.

What he must not do. Conclude that the unrecorded deed settles it, record the deed himself, tell the occupant the lien "won't matter because the deed is older," or market the property while the questions are open. The fourth is the one that turns a solvable title problem into a transaction with a buyer whose deadlines are running.

Why this lesson puts it here. Sections 1 through 5 supply every concept required to see the issues — deed requirements, delivery, recording, notice, priority, and what a preliminary report is. What they do not supply is the answer, and knowing the difference is the professional skill.

6.10 Involuntary transfer, and the four routes a title can move without a signature

Section 6.3 introduced involuntary transfer. The routes are worth having distinctly, because each leaves a different mark in a title chain and a licensee will meet all four.

RouteWhat happensWhat appears in the chain
ForeclosureThe security instrument's power is exercised; the property is soldA trustee's deed upon sale, or a sheriff's deed after judicial sale
Eminent domainA public agency takes for public use, paying just compensationA final order of condemnation, or a deed in lieu
Adverse possessionLong, open, hostile, exclusive possession under the statutory conditions, including payment of taxesNothing — until a quiet title judgment records it
EscheatAn owner dies with no heirs and no willA state proceeding and its judgment

And two more that move title without a conveyance from the owner:

Death. By will, or by intestate succession, or — where the vesting so provides — automatically to a surviving joint tenant under Civil Code § 683.

Court order. A dissolution judgment, a partition, a judgment of specific performance, a bankruptcy trustee's sale.
